subsubtopic: DIRECTIVE ISSUED RESPECTING SECURITY CLEARANCE OF PUBLIC SERVANTS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the terms of Standing Order 43. My motion relates to a directive which came out of the office of the Solicitor General with respect to the security clearance of people in sensitive and public positions.
A paragraph in the directive reads that no person can be cleared for such a position while he or she has close relatives living within the borders of such foreign nations as may cause subjection to intolerable pressures, or if he or she has recently resided in foreign countries where no check of activities is possible. Having regard to this, and since one-third of all Canadian citizens fall into this category, I ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges):
That the Solicitor General be required to rescind this directive immediately and avail himself at the earliest opportunity in the House of assuring hon. members that such clearances will not be carried out along ethnic lines.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on an urgent matter under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
Last night's CBC airing of the television drama "Drying Up the Streets" graphically brought to light the interrelated problems of heroin addiction and prostitution. In light of the concern about prostitution expressed yesterday in this House, and in light of the many requests made by myself and my colleagues for federal financial assistance to the British Columbia heroin health entry plan, a plan which is of considerable merit and which could lead toward the resolution of the heroin addiction problem in British Columbia, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen):
That this House recommends to the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, as well as the Solicitor General, that they request a special screening of "Drying Up the Streets" and that they spend some time with the Vancouver drug squad to witness first-hand the degradation and violence inherent in the heroin sub-culture and, further, this House recognizes the special drug problem of British Columbia by demonstrating its support for federal assistance to the British Columbia heroin health entry program.

NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT-SURPLUS OF NATURAL GAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources regarding the most recent report of the National Energy Board which indicates that if the board had followed the formula it has always used in the past, there would be no surplus of natural gas, but by means of a formula specially concocted for the occasion, it finds a surplus of 1.6 trillion cubic feet or 3.4 trillion cubic feet, depending on which premise is taken, and recommends an export of two trillion cubic feet.
In view of the fact the government has endorsed the idea of the Q and M line to the maritimes and the idea of making gas available to transfer from oil to gas in many of the industries in central Canada, can the minister assure the House and the country that no exports of natural gas will be approved until such time as it has been demonstrated that there is sufficient natural gas, first, for the Q and M line and, second, for the transfer from oil to gas in industry; and, finally, to supply the growing demands of the petrochemical industry for petroleum products?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT-SURPLUS OF NATURAL GAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, the government's priority has been to increase energy security for Canada; also, it has been to use natural gas to the maximum possible extent to displace foreign oil. For that reason, the government welcomes the findings of the National Energy Board that our
March 1, 1979

reserves have gone up significantly by 4.7 trillion cubic feet. There is absolutely record activity right now with respect to the exploration and development of our gas fields and petroleum resources.
The prospects for the future are exceedingly good. We are particularly pleased with all these events because they result from initiatives and a climate which the government has provided to get this kind of activity going.

subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT-SURPLUS OF NATURAL GAS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT-SURPLUS OF NATURAL GAS

Clearly, it is going to be possible for natural gas to provide a greater degree of energy security for Canadians than was thought to be the case a short while ago-two years ago-when the National Energy Board last reported. They have, as hon. members know, included two new tests along with the reserves test. We believe this deliverability test will be an improvement to the protection of Canadians in terms of future energy supply.
With the additional reserves, the additional tests and the possibility of using exports, as the hon. member has indicated, to maximize Canadian markets for natural gas, I think the outlook has changed quite significantly in the last two years.

subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT-SURPLUS OF NATURAL GAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that was a lot of gas, but not much of an answer to my question.
In view of the fact that in 1970 this government accepted the recommendation of the National Energy Board and approved the export of these three trillion cubic feet, and only a few years later the same board and the same government were telling the people of Canada that unless we built a pipeline into the Arctic we were going to freeze in the dark, the minister will have to find something better than this rhetoric in order to convince the Canadian people that we can meet our needs and at the same time export an additional two trillion cubic feet of natural gas.
I want to ask the minister this very specific question. In view of the fact that the estimate of Q and M for gas requirements is 5.1 trillion cubic feet, and the National Energy Board estimate is 3.3 cubic feet-which is a difference of 1.8 trillion cubic feet-and if Q and M is right in that regard, then two trillion cubic feet for export will be used up-and you cannot use the same gas twice-which will take priority, Q and M or the exports? Would the minister please answer that question?

subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT-SURPLUS OF NATURAL GAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have made it quite clear in answers in this House over the last few days, and even before, that the potential of the Q and M pipeline and the other competing application, the application by TransCanada PipeLines, to move Canadian gas into the Quebec and maritime markets is a matter of very great importance to this government.
I have just said, in answer to the hon. member's first question, that we believe that exports can also support that
Oral Questions
particular expansion of the Canadian market for Canadian gas. I think I made it very clear in my first answer that we would expect the National Energy Board, at its hearings, to examine the potential, the linkage between gas exports and the development of these markets in Canada.

subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT-SURPLUS OF NATURAL GAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, neither the National Energy Board nor anybody else, other than the government, can make the final determination as to which will have priority. I am trying to find out from the minister if Q and M is simply a pre-election gimmick for the people in the maritimes, or whether the government is serious in its intention to see to it that the gas available for that pipeline is reserves.
I want to tell the minister that page 5 of the National Energy Board report points out that in its previous report of two years ago it predicted we would have gas deficiencies by 1983, and it now says it is able to say that we will not have gas deficiencies before 1992. At my age, 1992 does not give me any concern, but to a blossoming youth like you, Mr. Speaker, it must cause some apprehension. I am, therefore, asking the minister if he considers that a 13-year down the road possibility of gas shortages does not concern him and does not make him feel that the government ought to say that the first priority for the gas which is now in place will be the Q and M line and the need for Canadian supplies, rather than the export market. Will the minister tell us where he stands on that?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT-SURPLUS OF NATURAL GAS

Mr. Speaker, I would like to go back over the same ground, because I think the hon. member has missed some of the important points I have made.
1 have stated many times my belief in the importance of the Q and M pipeline, or the competing application, to Canada. I have stated many times why I believe that the expansion of the gas markets in Quebec and the maritimes will be important to Canada, because it can displace foreign oil. I believe that the NEB makes this point, that natural gas can displace imported oil by as much as 100,000 barrels of oil per day by 1995. That is a very important factor in Canadian security.
The NEB, in their report, made it quite clear that they have taken my advice and the advice of the government with respect to this hearing, and they have made sure that there is sufficient gas to look after the expansion of eastern Canadian markets before they have looked at exports. I have gone further than that and said in my answers just a few moments ago that I would expect exports to be made as a result of the surplus which they have found.
Those exports could support the development and expansion of those markets in the way that, if we did not have any exports, we would not be able to support them. I think those exports could change the economic viability of the Q and M pipeline very considerably, and that is why I have said in my answers today that I believe export potential can be of very considerable help in moving that particular project forward.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have been a number of very significant increases in the allocation of moneys by the federal government for research and development in this country. Those were announced by my predecessor. At the same time, last summer, the government announced a number of measures aimed at securing more research and development in this country, and I refer to the Centre of Excellence policy.
At that time it was made quite clear that the increase in research and development, if we were to achieve the target of 1.5 per cent of the GNP by the early 1980s, would require a significant contribution from the private sector. The point was made that the government could not find the funds and spend the money to do it on its own; that it had to be done to a large extent in the private sector.
To that end, the Minister of Finance in his most recent budget changed, altered and improved the tax credit system for research and development in industry, a significant incremental change. I believe that the amounts there may be worth in the order of $125 million, and I very much hope that private industry will take advantage of this benefit.

Unfortunately, as a result of some technical defects we were unable to carry that through. Mr. Speaker, I am rising today in response to the question of privilege raised yesterday by the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick).
The essence of the hon. member's question of privilege relates to the fact that one paragraph was omitted in the English language copy of a letter dated June 26, 1978 from Mr. Guy Cousineau, president of Loto Canada, to myself concerning Loto Select. With respect to the omitted paragraph I have consulted Loto Canada on this matter and I have
Privilege-Mr. Dick
received a response from Mr. Cousineau, the president of the corporation, which reads as follows:
May I on behalf of Loto Canada apologize to you for the omission which occurred in Appendix B of the English copy of my report submitted to you and tabled in the House on February 21, 1979. The total report consists of a covering letter, an itemized account of the costs incurred in settling the Loto Select game, a copy of the settlement agreement with GIC and my letter to you dated June 26, 1978 on the Loto Select game. The material was tabled in both official languages.
In order to produce a report with typing uniformity, we employed an electromechanical process referred to as a Word Processing Machine. This process does not contain photocopying ability, therefore all the material had to be retyped into the Word Processing Machine and was re-signed with my signature stamp. Through a human error, the paragraph in question from my letter of June 26, 1978 was unfortunately omitted in the processing of the Appendix B of the English copy of my report. For this, and for any inconvenience caused to members of parliament, I again apologize.
The Appendix B in the French copy of my report did include the paragraph in question from my letter of June 26, 1978 which repudiates suggestions that there was any intent to mislead.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a separate question of privilege. Today in her question of privilege the minister made great point of the fact that someone on this side claimed she had misled deliberately the House or Canadian people. I can understand, if such a claim had been made, that the minister would be quite properly upset. That is why I am particularly disturbed by the fact that during oral question period today the minister made exactly that charge against me.
In response to a question which I put to the minister during oral question period today, she said that I appeared continually to refer to the amount of $13.15 million expended on Loto Select as a loss, that I attempted to attribute it to the General Instrument contract alone, and then she said "which he knows well is false".
At this point I will not digress into the question of the veracity of the minister's statement where she claimed that I indicated all of the $13 million she wasted had been wasted on the General Instrument contract. I well know that figure is $8 million and that she wasted $5 million elsewhere. Of course, I at no time indicated that the whole of the $13 million wasted was wasted on the one contract.
The procedural point here, which I think is very important, is that the minister claimed I deliberately gave information which I knew to be false. On the basis of all the precedents I have seen, an imputation made by one member against another that a member deliberately would mislead the House constitutes a breach of privilege. I think the onus is upon the minister to withdraw that statement and enter an apology for it.
If it would be useful, I could make available various precedents in which it is made quite clear that it is totally improper for one member to accuse another of deliberately misleading the House or deliberately making statements which he knows to be false. I would be prepared to do that if Mr. Speaker felt

it was useful, but I am sure the precedents are so well known to all members of the House, including the minister, that they do not need to be cited by me now. When the minister said "which he well knows is false", no other construction can be put on it than that she is accusing me of having misled the House deliberately. Clearly that is a breach of my privileges as a member of the House.

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, February 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ouellet that Bill C-29, to amend the National Housing Act and Central Mortgage and Housing Act and to make other related amendments, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, just prior to calling it six o'clock last evening I was speaking about the CHIP program which provides grants for insulation.


March 1, 1979
1 am delighted to see the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) here this afternoon and I welcome him.
Let me point out again that this is a program in respect of which we should be spending more money. I hope the department is doing a good job publicizing the advantages of this program, as I have been trying to do.
I am also hoping that the minister will relent and treat the rest of Canada in the same way he is treating Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island by allowing the full $500 grant. The minister can wipe the tears from his eyes. There are many people in other parts of Canada who are just as much in need of the $500 grant. 1 might also point out that the $500 grant in other parts of Canada is subject to income tax. It has to be added to taxable income and I certainly do not think that is fair. I hope the minister will give serious consideration to changing this provision. It is very difficult to get an application processed. I am still receiving a great many phone calls and applications, all of which have to be channelled through Montreal. As I have stated before, I think this whole thing would be handled more expeditiously if the minister would allocate this insulation program responsibility to the CMHC offices throughout the country.
I spoke this afternoon to people at two of these offices in my riding, one at North Bay and one at Barrie. I was told their only input was, in response to requests on a hit and miss basis, to make inspections in respect of allowed grants.
Let me emphasize the need for public housing in rural areas. A large segment of our population is still living in rural areas and is still in need of adequate housing. My own village of Burks Falls, where I served as reeve for 26 years, was one of the first municipalities in the area to take the initiative in providing housing for senior citizens, as well as low rental housing. Over ten years ago, and this probably is not very much, four senior citizens' units were built along with four low rental housing units. Just prior to my election to the House of Commons in 1972, our municipal council had obtained approval to build an additional senior citizens' apartment complex of 23 units and five low rental housing units. I am delighted to say that these units are completed and fully occupied.
I mention these examples to drive home two basic and important points to the government. The first is the case to be made for the forgotten or non-urban part of Canada-in other words, the rural areas. The second point is that these exemplary initiatives on the part of this small village serve to point out the need for a social element in the housing policy. Our senior citizens have devoted many of their best years, their young and dynamic years, to building this country. Many have made significant contributions in the defence and security of this country through service in the armed forces.
I would like to take this opportunity to pay special tribute to the Canadian Legion in my village of Burks Falls, which is sponsoring another senior citizens' complex of 25 units, and I hope that it will receive approval. We of later generations owe a debt of deep gratitude to them and also comfortable living
Housing
during retirement. It is for this reason that I have on a number of occasions spoken on improved conditions for our senior citizens. Today I would urge the government not to neglect the many in this group who do not have the means to acquire satisfactory and adequate shelter, and to render every assistance possible.
There is another element of society which is having difficulty, and I believe that it is a problem which is occurring more in the smaller towns and villages rather than in the cities. I refer, of course, to the physically handicapped who find it difficult to get houses in which they are able to get around satisfactorily. I have with me a news item from the Gravenhurst News dated February 22. I would like to point out to the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) that, while I realize that the delivery of weekly newspapers is not very good across Canada and particularly not in Ontario, this particular newspaper left Gravenhurst on the 22nd and lo and behold arrived in my office yesterday. I know the Postmaster General will be delighted to hear that this weekly paper arrived within a week after posting, whereas many of them are delivered considerably later than that.
The news article takes the form of a letter to the editor and is headed "Physically handicapped face desperate housing problem". It reads:
I am writing to you to inform the residents of Muskoka of a problem that exists in this area.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, there are many other areas where there is this problem of suitable housing for the physically handicapped.
There has been provisions made for the senior citizens, mentally handicapped, physically handicapped that cannot take care of themselves and for people on low incomes.
The government and municipalities have done a good job for these people, although it took some persuasion.
I now feel that the physically handicapped who are married with a family need single level housing or apartments that have elevators so that the ones in wheelchairs or who are unable to climb excessive amounts of stairs have proper housing.
Most people that are physically handicapped are on pensions. These pensions are usually very small, similar in fact to the senior citizens. Some of us are, in fact, on welfare where a family of four are given $429 a month to live on.
Some of us are injured on the job trying to do what our employers want, like myself lifting equipment that's too heavy and injured my back. Others through auto accidents; the ways to get injured are too many to mention, but it shows it could happen to anyone.
The article goes on to outline the needs of these people:
Luckily for me there was an area that I could put a bed in.
He is referring to his own house, and he goes on to describe how he was able to make do. The article continues:
This along with the rent, utilities and other bills, a place that is one level and geared to income would be a blessing. I don't know how many more are in the same situation as I am but we that are in this situation need help. If people would write to their member of parliament, mayor, town council or anyone that might be able to help, I know I would appreciate it and I think many more would also.
Thank you for reading this and be thankful for your health.
The article was written by William Manary of Gravenhurst. He will certainly find that his letter has received some publici-
3722

March 1, 1979
Housing
ty. I personally have not received a letter from him, but in all probability I will be writing him in answer to his request.
Another important area of housing where the government ought to provide encouragement is in the building of energy saving devices into new homes in Canada. The federal government should provide the lead and assistance in this area. I will relate one disturbing example of the bureaucratic set-up which some manufacturers of energy saving devices are up against. One could import an energy-saving device package from the United States, an item which is exempt from federal sales tax. But if parts of an energy saving device are bought individually in Canada, they are subject to federal sales tax. This is grossly unfair, not only to the consumer but to the small manufacturers in Canada. The government could easily require assurances from suppliers and users that a part sold will be used as a part of an energy-saving device and thus be exempt from federal sales tax.
Solar heating along with heating pumps should also be encouraged in the form of tax exemptions or deductions, or possibly in the case of new homes grants could be paid out. The Progressive Conservative party has already gone on record that they will bring to parliament, after the next election when they become the government, legislation which will allow tax credits for owner occupied homes that instal solar heat up to a maximum of $2,100.
CMHC is in the process of becoming a land-owning baron with control over large and luxurious pieces of property. Given the minister's lust for power in any form, the desire to acquire as much inventory for CMHC as possible comes as no surprise. The establishment of the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs has not in any substantial way alleviated many of the hardships resulting from inadequate or poor shelter. When
280,000	families in Canada pay more than 50 per cent of their family income for housing, 500,000 families pay more than 35 per cent, and another 820,000 families pay more than 25 per cent, and when two-thirds of those Canadians in need of housing cannot afford to buy or rent a home without a government subsidy, one begins to question the policies of the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs, and specifically, of CMHC. The state of housing in this country is a serious problem and affects each one of us in a very human and financial manner.
The unhealthy state of the economy has had its effect on the housing sector as well. The desperate attempts by the federal government to salvage the declining Canadian dollar has resulted in higher interest rates to attract foreign funds. In the process, however, mortgage rates have also skyrocketed. The graduated payment mortgage program involving a payment reduction is merely a juggling of figures and not a solution to the root of inflation and mismanagement in housing. This scheme may serve as a rude awakening to many at a later time, if they become accustomed to low monthly payments and then are later confronted with high monthly payments.
Another important facet in housing is our native and rural housing. In the field of native housing the federal government has a long way to go to meet its obligations to native people in

Canada. I recall that some years ago the government made the great promise that 50,000 units would be allocated for native housing. I have had the privilege of serving on our housing committee for as long as most members, almost six years, and over those years the government has conducted one survey after another to determine housing needs on Indian reserves. The native people are still awaiting the implementation of the results of these surveys. The money designated for upgrading housing for native people has probably been spent by the federal government on building palaces across the river in Hull to house 20,000 civil servants.
The federal government should encourage funding and subsidy housing programs at the band level which will create job opportunities on the reserves. The government has failed to award the majority of contracts to those willing to generate employment among the residents of reserves.
To meet the goal of adequate housing for our native people an annual construction rate of 4,500 new units and approximately 6,000 major renovations per year are required. Currently, the annual average construction rate is merely 2,400 units and only a small number-1,800 units per year-are being renovated. This obviously falls far short of the necessity to meet the goal of providing adequate housing for our native people.
There has also been a housing program for native and non-status Indian and rural people. In my area there is one such subdivision. The individual who was going to develop the property purchased it and made his first overtures to the government in 1961. He was told there was no need for it. Finally, it got under way about 18 months ago after consultation with the CMHC office in North Bay. Five homes have been completed and another three are almost complete, but so far the builder has not received any money from CMHC.
I concede it is not all the fault of CMHC because other levels of government have participated in the project. The Ontario government held up final approval through the Department of the Environment. Those of us who are aware of the problems of builders and developers know that in a great many cases the municipal governments are the culprits. It would be a good thing if a limit could be put on the length of time a government department may hold up a subdivision, and if they did not provide a proper answer within a reasonable period of time, then automatic approval would be given.
The subdivision I refer to entailed an outlay of $300,000 with the homes being in the $35,000 to $36,000 bracket. The local builder and developer has had to pay all the bills and be responsible for the financing for the past 18 months. Naturally, these costs will be levied against the ultimate homeowner and in all probability will cut down on the profit. I am delighted to be able to inform the House that some units were also built in Parry Sound in the same period.
In my riding the AHOP program is too expensive and very few, if any, houses were built, although the RRAP programs have been successful. In Muskoka 120 different RRAP pro-
March 1, 1979

grams were approved and in Parry Sound 25 RRAP programs were approved. I commend the government for this.
It is interesting to note that in the town of Gravenhurst there was an aggressive program to make certain that they took advantage of every government program and every housing project that was available. They are to be commended for this. The former clerk-treasurer, Mr. Ted Soucie, was an expert in this field. Perhaps he was too good because Gravenhurst lost him to the city of Orillia where he is now co-ordinator of housing. I am sure Orillia will do very well under his direction.
I understand that the municipality of Bracebridge is getting housing programs under way. I hope that one of the banner towns in my riding, Huntsville, will look into this and take advantage of any opportunities.
We are all well aware of the confusion brought about by the federal government's move to introduce metric conversion, or probably I should say metric confusion. Beginning May 1, it will be mandatory for all applications under the National Housing Act to use the metric system so as to conform to the directive issued by CMHC.
My colleague, the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil), expressed concern on behalf of the housing and lumber industry very eloquently in the adjournment debate last Monday, February 19. The concern is very legitimate and obvious. About 80 per cent of our lumber trade is with the United States and they have not yet converted to metric. They are being allowed the option whether to convert to metric or not, while we in Canada have been told it is mandatory. I could mention the millions and millions of dollars this metric program will cost Canadian businessmen in every walk of life.
I want to refer briefly, Mr. Speaker, to the remarks by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs in Toronto about a week ago. The minister made desperate attempts to spell out a housing policy on behalf of his Liberal colleagues. Needless to say, he fell flat on his face. When cornered by the press to further explain the specifics of his statements, the minister took shelter by stating that he was merely "thinking out aloud" some of the concepts which as yet have not been discussed by the federal government. This clearcut confession on the part of the minister, Mr. Speaker, comes closest to affirming the fears of many Canadians that this government lacks any well thought out policy on housing.
In the same speech, in trying to make a case for a shelter allowance system, the minister stated that this will be done "in the near future, as soon as our economy permits". Mr. Speaker, I ask how can the minister in all honesty proceed to announce the implementation of certain policies while at the same time introduce a clause such as "as soon as our economy permits"? I hope the minister does not tell his landlord that he will pay the rent as soon as his personal finances permit, or go to a store and purchase items with a promise to pay when the minister gets rich-or perhaps, I should say richer.
Canadians have responded overwhelmingly to the housing policies outlined by the Progressive Conservative party. Our
Housing
housing policy will benefit both home owners and tenants and, as well, provide much needed economic stimulus.
Nothing could be more beneficial to the housing industry than the proposal by my party to allow deductibility of up to a maximum of $5,000 on mortgage interest payments. Under this far-reaching proposal local property taxes will also be made deductible up to a maximum of $1,000 a year.
I take great delight in our mortgage and tax deductibility plan, Mr. Speaker. I was a member of a municipal council for a great many years. I served as a vice-president of the Ontario mayors and reeves-which is now the Association of Municipalities of Ontario-association for some years which continuously brought this resolution before the convention which comprised 900 municipalities in Ontario. The resolution was passed every time and I certainly had something to do with bringing it forward in the first place. It referred to municipal tax deductions only but I welcome the fact that this party, because of the high rate of mortgage interest at the present time, has seen fit to include mortgage interest also.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Hugh A. Anderson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 took great interest in the comments of my good friend from Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling). Perhaps I might comment on one portion of his speech with regard to the apparent lack of progress on the issue of native housing. I wonder whether the hon. member is aware that for the first time in the history of Canada, through Bill C-29, loans may be insured when made to Indians living on reserves, be they individuals, groups or bands, to help them buy, improve or build housing projects on those reserves.
Up until the present time, and until this bill is passed, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner) is charged with the responsibility of guaranteeing loans made to bands, individuals or groups and making payment should default occur. The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has had a problem in this area, because the finances of the department are not set up in such a way as to enable the department to enter into large scale housing projects.
Under Bill C-29-and I hope the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka agrees with this concept-this responsibility will be taken out of the hands of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and placed where it rightly belongs, under the guarantee program of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This means that when loans are made for use on reserves, whether to individuals, groups or band councils, CMHC will be the guarantor. Therefore, CMHC will be able to have more construction go ahead on reserves. Some of the constraints previously placed on the program due to the fact that housing on Indian reserves had to be guaranteed by the Minister of Indian Affairs will be

March 1, 1979
Housing
removed. I hope the hon. member will agree that that is a step in the right direction. I see he is nodding his head.
I do not want to give a political speech on the question of mortgage deductibility. However, I ask the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka and the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway) in all seriousness whether they would stand up in this House and say on the question of native housing on reserves whether the interest deductibility brought forth by the Conservative party will apply to Indian housing. I think both hon. members would have to agree that the deductibility of mortgage interest would not affect Indian housing one iota. Bill C-29, whereby CMHC will guarantee loans on reserves, is a far better method of attacking that problem.
It is not the only way.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Hon. members are no doubt aware that through the department of Indian affairs we already have a $12,000 grant system for each home that qualifies to be built on reserves where funds are available. What I am speaking about is in addition to what CMHC guarantees. We all agree that housing on reserves is inadequate. Therefore, the government has addressed that problem. There will now be a better weapon to attack it by making much larger funds available to Indian housing.
I would like briefly to review what has occurred to bring us up to the point where Bill C-29 is now in front of the House. In 1978 the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) announced a series of changes in federal government housing policy which were the result of a number of consultations that had taken place between the provinces and the federal government.
The first objective of government housing policy at that time was to maintain a high level of housing production. Hon. members will recall in the 1974-75 period the former minister of urban affairs set up a four-year program. The target was to construct 250,000 houses per year over a four-year period. That program was announced in order that contractors could be made aware of the government's policy. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson), who is now in the chamber, was minister of urban affairs at that time. The government of Canada said it would build one million homes over a four year period. That objective has been met. The present Minister of State for Urban Affairs says that he wants to maintain that high level of housing production started by the former minister.
It was also targeted in May, 1978 to increase the number of non-profit housing units to be constructed per year from
19,000	to 30,000. The philosophy was that the government thrust in housing policy should be in those areas where people have the greatest needs and the least income. That was the second point brought forward in May, 1978.
The third point has not been discussed during the debate on Bill C-29. It is something we all agree is desirable. I refer to the disentanglement of the complex set of arrangements under federal and provincial housing regulations which had been operating over a number of years.

The fourth point brought forward by the Liberal government-and my friends across the aisle will be very surprised to hear this-was to utilize the capital that exists in the private sector. I think even the Conservative party could live with that objective. The capital sitting in our banks and trust companies would be utilized to the fullest possible extent rather than using government funds.
What did we propose to meet those four objectives? First, we brought in new non-profit housing programs. We said at that time that we would operate a program through non-profit corporations, whether they be private corporations such as the Lions Club, Kiwanis and organizations like that or whether we deal through municipal or provincial governments. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka brought up a good point. Very seldom in this House are organizations such as the Lions Club, Kiwanis or Rotary Club recognized for the great contribution they make.
And the Legion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
And the Legion. They sponsor senior citizens housing projects, organize them and accept the lead thrust in setting up those programs. I thank the hon. member for bringing this to our attention. These organizations have sponsored a great number of projects for senior citizens across this country.
What did we say we would do? At the present time CMHC through government funds provides 50-year mortgages for senior citizen housing complexes at a rate slightly below the prime interest rate. That has been going on for the past number of years. They get 90 per cent financing. In other words, the organizations had to provide up to 10 per cent of the cost of the project. The other 90 per cent was financed by the federal government under CMHC with 50-year mortgages repayable at a rate of interest in the neighbourhood of 9 per cent.
We said that 19,000 units per year were not enough, that would bring in a better bill and utilize funds from the private sector by cutting off CMHC funds to those organizations. The banks and trust companies told us they had adequate funds on deposit to handle the situation. So under the new arrangement the banks and trust companies would provide not 90 per cent but 100 per cent of the financing.
Most hon. members are aware that interest rates are high these days. If we had just left it at that, with the banks and trust companies lending the money at these high interest rates, it would have been very difficult to provide housing for senior citizens or others whose incomes are restricted. What the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) undertook to do was to subsidize through the Bank of Canada so as to bring down the current rate of interest, whatever it was, to as low as 2 per cent. In other words, the Kiwanis, the Legion branches or any of those groups which do this great work would benefit from a subsidy which would reduce the current interest rate to 2 per cent.
March 1, 1979

We believe an initiative of this sort would make it easier for the organizations concerned. First, they will not have to worry about paying interest rates of 10 per cent or so and, second, they would be able to reduce the length of the mortgage. Because if they are not paying 9 per cent or 10 per cent, more funds can be devoted to repayment of principle. This, we believe, will stimulate the construction of senior citizens' housing.
The solution which hon. members opposite have proposed is to allow deductibility of mortgage interest and municipal taxes paid by senior citizens. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, whether the plans which have been put forward by the government in Bill C-29 are not a better source of funding, a better way of stimulating the construction of senior citizens' housing. 1 suspect even hon. members opposite will agree that our plan is better because it goes much further to assist people living on low or fixed incomes than the proposal advanced by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark).
There is a second aspect to Bill C-29 and it concerns community service programs. Many of us are aware that an assistance program for municipalities has been in place in the form of the Canada Works program. We have been putting in sidewalks, rural electrification, scout halls, a variety of items which are of assistance to municipalities, providing 100 per cent funding for labour on selected projects. We realize this does not meet the need completely because we are not dealing with capital cost for such things as the erection of libraries, museums, parks, swimming pools and skating rinks, for example, which are so important a part of the facilities communities try to provide for their residents.
We have on a number of occasions provided programs to assist municipalities, realizing that in many cases provinces were not able to address this need. In May, 1978, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs announced a global approach in assistance for community services. For some years the federal government had been providing assistance to provinces and municipalities with respect to neighbourhood improvements, sewage treatment plants, the installation of water lines, medium density housing and so on. What the minister is proposing in Bill C-29 is an expansion and consolidation of this assistance under a program called the community services program. The object is to provide increased flexibility and wider latitude to the provinces and their municipalities in using federal funds, to enable federal assistance better to respond to local needs and conditions and to reduce duplication in administration by disentangling the federal government from project-by-project scrutiny.
What is even more important is that it seeks to enhance the degree to which federal assistance meets the priorities of the provinces and the municipalities and ensure that it is available equally to all provinces. Funding under the community services program will be used not only for neighbourhood improvements and water and sewage treatment for medium density housing, but for building social, cultural and recreational facilities, such as day care centres, community centres, libraries, neighbourhood ice rinks and parks.
Housing
Most members here have been asking for some method of funding recreational activities, day care centres, community centres, libraries, parks and so on. Well, there was a program a number of years ago called the winter works program which was capital intensive. That program was dropped, but I believe that with the community services program, the Canada Works program and the Young Canada Works program we shall be able to address the needs of communities to a much greater extent than in the past.
Most hon. members recognize that communities do experience a real and pressing need for services to be provided to their people. However, in larger cities such as Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver this need may not be so pressing as in smaller communities because, after all, they do have a large tax base. I see I have the Minister of National Defence on my side; 1 have probably got him offside now! But there are many communities with populations of 500, or not much more than
1,000,	which do not really have a tax base large enough to enable their residents to enjoy some of the amenities which Canadians in the larger centres sometimes take for granted.
It has always been my contention that if the government wants to see more people living in the smaller centres, it will have to make a conscious effort to assist these small communities so that they can retain their populations. Unless some of the amenities of life are provided, people will likely move to the larger centres. I might point out that it was only some 18 months ago that television service was brought to the northern part of my riding, and I would remind the House that I do not represent a constituency in the Yukon or in the Northwest Territories cities; I represent upper Vanvouver Island. It is only within the last 18 months that the lumber and mining communities of northern Vancouver Island got a CBC repeater. Small though they may be, these communities have a very important role to play in our society. We should be attempting to attract people to these communities to work in the mining industry.
On northern Vancouver Island there is a mine called the Utah mine, which is the largest open pit copper mine in Canada. However, it was only 18 months ago that we got a repeater in there. It is hard to tell people to come and live on northern Vancouver Island when only a few months ago there was no road connecting northern Vancouver Island with southern Vancouver Island. There was no television to watch. Many of the communities did not have community halls for recreation. I think this part of Bill C-29 will assist such small, remote communities perhaps to an even greater extent than it will assist larger centres, because I think we will be able to provide services to those small and remote communities. I hope it is the intention of the federal and provincial governments to maintain these areas.
I suspect that in coming parliaments, regardless of what the government of the day might be, there will have to be direct assistance to people living in small and isolated communities. Otherwise we will have a group of city states where the

March 1, 1979
Housing
population will be centred and where crime will be on the increase because of jamming more and more people together. I hope future parliaments in conjunction with the provinces will look very closely not only at maintaining small rural centres but also enlarging their roles and enhancing their facilities so that people will continue to reside in them and not be drawn like a magnet to the city states of Vancouver, Montreal and Toronto. I suspect that if we were to look at Alberta we would find the same thing happening in Edmonton and Calgary, and if we were to look at Saskatchewan we might find the same thing happening in the cities of Saskatoon and Regina.
I have heard federal and provincial governments paying lip service to the idea that we do not want all the people in Canada living in small city states or large city states. We have said that. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka and I have both debated this. Both of us have brought this to the attention of the House on numerous occasions, because there is a concern in rural Canada about people being drained off.
Let me give an example. We talk about a decentralization program for the federal government under which we move civil servants out of Ottawa. Where do we move them to?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: We move them to cities like Edmonton, Calgary, Saskatoon, Regina-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
-or Vancouver. We who make decisions, presumably for the benefit of the country, in our own wisdom are furthering a centralization program, not in Ottawa but in the city states I have named. There is absolutely no need to transfer civil servants out of Ottawa to Vancouver. Vancouver already has a housing problem. There is a shortage of land.
The provinces also have a role to play. All industry seems to be located in areas such as Hamilton, Toronto and Vancouver. When it comes to setting up new facilities, whether they be brand new plants or expansions, some consideration must be given to the idea that every plant and every branch plant cannot be built in already crowded cities. I think the provinces have a very large role to play in this.
In my province of British Columbia the concentration of population and industry is within a few miles of the lower mainland and the greater Vancouver and greater Victoria areas. There has to be a change. If jobs are not created in small communities such as Nanaimo, Port Alberni, Courtenay, Campbell River or Port Hardy, which are small communities on Vancouver Island, the sons and daughters of the people living in those areas will be forced to leave. They will be forced to seek work in such places as Victoria and Vancouver. That will cause more problems for transit systems. It will cause policing problems, problems for fire departments and urban planning difficulties. There is a role for the federal government in this, and there is also a role for provincial governments.
In Bill C-29 an attempt is being made by the federal government to provide community service programs which, I

re-emphasize, will benefit small communities with small tax bases more than it will benefit larger communities. For that reason I am pleased to support this legislation.
There are other aspects of the legislation which are important but upon which I have not touched. I will leave those aspects to other hon. members.
I would like to say something regarding the question of mortgage interest deductibility and municipal tax deductibility of up to $1,000 which is being proposed by the Conservative party. I suppose many Canadians look at politicians with some jaundice. I suppose there are good reasons why Canadians look at us somewhat askance. In 1978 we had a federal deficit of which most of us on both sides of the House were not very proud.
In 1978 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Government of Canada announced that government spending would be reduced by $2 billion in 1979. I have sat in this House for the last four and a half years and listened to hon. members opposite tell us that we are financially irresponsible and spending too much money.
Right.
Right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: There were two "rights" there but no "wrongs." When an election looms on the horizon those same proponents of financial responsibility jump up on their hind legs and say that they would have twice the deficit we have now. The point is that the boy who would be king is attempting to win an election by bribing the electorate of Canada. He would allow the deficit to be increased, and he would pass it on to our children and grandchildren. Hon. members opposite propose that. Are they telling us that a mortgage interest deduction and a municipal tax deduction will not create a higher deficit? The Leader of the Opposition told the people of Canada that what his party is proposing is a constructive deficit.
Don't talk about ours. Tell us about yours, all $12 billion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thought hon. members opposite were at least-
Let's hear about your deficit.
Order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
I realize the hon. members opposite do not like being criticized, but all I am asking is that the people of Canada ask themselves whether they want a higher deficit at this point. That is the paramount question. Even the Leader of the Opposition admits that this program would cost in excess of $2 billion initially. Total cost after a four-year period when the entire program would be in effect can only be estimated. It has been estimated by one source that it would cost the people of Canada up to $4 billion.
March 1, 1979

It is said often in Canada that there is very little difference between the Liberal and Conservative parties.
Vive la difference.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
I suppose that is one example of the difference in philosophy that exists between the two parties. The government says that our housing policy should be directed at people on the lower end of the income scale. The programs about which I spoke were for the senior citizens. It is our attempt to answer the very real need for housing of our senior citizens. When I referred to what was happening on the reserves, this is our approach to dealing with a very difficult problem. I repeat that the Liberal government's housing policy is aimed at helping people at the lower end of the income scale on the assumption that people at the high end of the income scale do not require the same assistance.
The difference between the two parties is that the Conservative party has come up with the brilliant idea that it is not the native people, the senior citizens and young couples starting married life who need that assistance. What the Conservative party in its wisdom has come up with is that it is people who earn more than $20,000 a year who need that assistance. I hope that the people of Canada on election day, which I hope will come shortly, will decide whether or not this is an election gimmick and who will benefit from that scheme. I will campaign on Bill C-29, and I suppose the hon. member will campaign on giving more money to those people who already have it.
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. Would the hon. member entertain a question?
That is not a point of order. Would the parliamentary secretary entertain a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: I would be very pleased to entertain a question, except that I am catching a taxi at a quarter to five to get back to my riding.
This is not Friday.

Mr. Speaker, the housing bill that is before us today is an example of the withdrawal of the Liberal government from the serious commitment to help Canadians with affordable housing. It reflects the acceptance by the Liberal party of the Conservative idea of restraint and cutback in government spending. Because when you analyse what is in the bill, Mr. Speaker, you can only conclude that the government has reduced the amount of money for certain programs to assist the development of housing in Canada and has further restricted the scope of programming that is already on the books. Having listened to the debate I must conclude that it is a case between Liberal and Conservative members of Tweedle-dum saying to Twee-dle-dee "I am different from you." In reality there is not that much difference.
Housing
When one looks at the bill, one finds that government is initiating a withdrawal of its lending policy through CMHC and letting the private sector take over the responsibility. It also shows that the government has embarked on a withdrawal from supporting and building public housing and cutting back on low income housing. The bill shows clearly that the government intends to cut back on assistance to middle-class housing.
I will discuss the details of the bill more thoroughly in committee, but let me point out that we find, in summary, that the bill ends the generous aid to co-ops and non-profit housing which was initiated during the minority parliament in response to the pressure that the NDP was able to put on the government at that time and replaces these programs and this assistance with less expensive or less generous subsidies to co-ops and non-profit housing. This program will bring an end to rent supplements on the fifty-fifty federal-provincial sharing basis for co-ops, non-profit housing and provincial or municipal housing.
It will also end loans to provinces or municipalities for the construction of public housing and the fifty-fifty sharing of operating losses in such projects. CMHC will continue to offer provinces a partnership arrangement in public housing. The federal government will pay 75 per cent of capital cost and operating losses. The trouble is, of course, that the provinces do not care very much for this option and their initial response has not been very enthusiastic.
As I said, this bill will bring an end to assisted home ownership and assisted rental programs. It will introduce the graduated payment mortgage, insured but not offered by CMHC. Like AHOP, it simply postpones the monthly mortgage payment you cannot afford to make anyway.
The bill expands the type of mortgages which CMHC can insure to make up for the fact that CMHC no longer lends money. The bill will expand the residential rehabilitation program, but without sufficient funds to implement it in the way it should be, and it will end the municipal infrastructure program for water and sewers, the municipal incentive program and grants for medium density housing. It will end the neighbourhood improvement program and replace it with the community services program which, contrary to what the previous speaker said, provides less money for a wider range of projects.
In my constituency of Sault Ste. Marie, our municipality is quite concerned about getting federal aid to expand and develop a second sewage treatment plant in the western part of the city and also to extend the water main services to areas in the northern part of the city. I am afraid that because of the Liberal government's policy of adopting the Tory philosophy of restraint and cutback, the funds for our city will be pretty tight if it wants to implement these much needed improvements in sewer and water main construction. I am continuing to lobby with the government and the minister to give our city some priority on this and I pledge to my constituents that I will continue to do so.
When we look at the housing situation today, we find that there is only one phrase which can accurately describe it, and

March 1, 1979
Housing
that is that we are facing a housing crisis, a crisis in terms of affordable shelter. Government statistics show that over one third of Canadian households, or over one million Canadians in actual numbers, are suffering from some kind of housing deprivation; that is to say, either inadequate or overcrowded housing or housing which costs more than 25 per cent of the total income. The figure of 25 per cent is a universally accepted standard. If you pay more than 25 per cent of your income for shelter, it is unacceptable in terms of your budget; you are spending too much on shelter and having to go without other essentials such as food and clothing.
It is a shameful situation in Canada today. Many citizens of large municipalities such as Montreal, Toronto and some others where there are many problems with finding adequate, affordable housing are spending more than 25 per cent of their income on shelter. We find that 547,000 Canadians are in that category. It is a shameful situation in terms of the reality of housing today. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) has stood up in the House and said what great progress has been made; but the reality, those cold, hard figures which represent human beings, cannot be denied by this government, and I hope that during this election campaign we will be able to drive that message home.
The reality is that home ownership is becoming or has become too expensive for thousands and thousands of Canadians. It has become too expensive especially for young couples. I have talked with many young couples and parents of young couples, and they said that they do not know how they will ever attain the goal or dream of owning an individual family household, a home in which to raise their children with some sense of comfort and decency. Even if young couples have incomes of some $14,000 to $17,000 a year, how many of them can afford the $385 a month mortgage payment it takes to pay off a 25-year mortgage of $40,000 at the current interest rate of some 11 per cent? That is the reality for young couples today who want to own homes.
In my constituency of Sault Ste. Marie the average monthly mortgage payment is $400. For most home owners it means that both the husbands and wives have to work if they are to meet their mortgage payments. Indeed, the manager of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in Sault Ste. Marie said that 99 per cent of the couples or individuals coming to him for mortgage assistance are faced with situations where both spouses have to work in order to make ends meet. Many young couples today cannot afford the mortgage costs for an average home because of their actual incomes or because one spouse cannot find a job. Therefore, in many cases they raise their children in a crowded environment.
Another group really hurt by the housing situation today, of course, is senior citizens, pensioners and those on very low incomes. They need assisted housing and senior citizens' apartments. They need rent geared to income units built by governments at all three levels. Yet we see what is happening at the federal level. The government professes to have some concern

for and commitment to Canadians, but we find it gradually withdrawing and pulling out of an active and meaningful involvement in building housing units and accommodations which many people desperately need.
If we are to get at the central problem of high housing costs, we must analyse what pushes these costs up and then try to deal with the factors in a rational and sound manner. In the course of my speech I should like to examine the key factors and whether government can take any action to bring down or hold down the rising costs which are making housing unaffordable.
First we can look at some recent statistics. Housing prices doubled between 1971 and 1976. We must look at some of these factors, one being the cost of construction. One cannot deny that the cost of building a house has gone up. In the period from 1971 to 1976, the cost of materials rose 65 per cent. Recently in the House I raised the issue of the high cost of lumber. The price of lumber has gone up 70 per cent in the past two years. This adds approximately $1,200 in cost to the average size house with a floor space of 1,800 square feet.
I have pressed the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand) to take some kind of action to stop this price rip-off. The cost of production for lumber has not gone up. What has happened is that the world and American markets are demanding wood at such increasing rates that companies are charging whatever those markets will bear, as well as charging the same prices in Canada. The government sits by and does nothing about it.
There are various policies and initiatives which could be taken. Perhaps the best would be to implement a two-price system so that we in Canada will not be paying the high world price for something we produce here. The cost of materials has gone up. The government could take action to stop that escalation, but it is a toothless tiger when it comes to protecting consumers and home buyers.
The second cost is that of labour. Wages in the construction industry have gone up some 80 per cent in the period from 1971 to 1976. Some hon. members, especially Conservative and Liberal ones, would say, "Perhaps we should have held down the wages of these workers". They would argue that despite the fact that during the same period of time the cost of living rose 75 per cent. Somehow these workers would have been required to bear the burden of inflation by not trying to keep up with it. Of course, that is an unacceptable solution. Nevertheless, that fact is that the cost of labour has gone up, as everything else has.
The third reason housing is so expensive today is what has happened to interest rates. In 1971 interest rates ranged around an average of 5.25 per cent. In January, 1978, the interest rate was 11.25 per cent. That is some record during this Trudeau administration! It should be noted also that while these interest rates were going up, something dramatic was happening to bank profits. After all taxes had been paid, bank profits increased some 159 per cent during that same period of time. The increase alone in 1978 over 1977 was some 33 per cent in profits, representing almost $1 billion. Yet that trend
March 1, 1979

was never countered, nor were any attempts made by the government to slow it down or to bring to bear some type of moderating influence on actual interest rates.
The government has implemented various kinds of subsidy programs for certain groups in terms of Canadian taxpayers subsidizing the person with a mortgage by giving him a lower mortgage, with the bank receiving the going rate. But that is not a solution for the majority of people who want to own homes. Thus we see the cost of money has been a major factor in this tremendous increase in the cost of home ownership.
There is another reason for the current housing cost, and that is the cost of land. Mr. Speaker, may I call it five o'clock? I will resume debate later this evening.
