Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
That an Order of the House do issue for a copy of the approximately 1600 job studies in the construction trades across Canada prepared in order to update the Canadian Classification and Dictionary of Occupants and contracted to South-am Business Publications, Don Mills, Ontario.
He said: Mr. Speaker, when I became aware that this study was going on, my interest was activated because, as many of the members of the House know, before I came here as a member of parliament I was in the construction industry. Possibly some members would suggest that I should go back to the construction industry. 1 was interested because I wondered what they were doing and why they were doing it, so I asked for the papers and was told by the parliamentary secretary that he could not comply with the motion since the information on jobs that they had asked the contractors to gather for the studies may in many instances be regarded as confidential.
1 know that on many occasions I have found that the persons answering had not seen the papers in question, and in many cases some of us have seen papers that are marked confidential. The problem I have arises often from the fact that no one is willing to make a decision that the papers really are not that important and could quite easily be released.
My interest stemmed originally from looking at the document for which the study was being made. I read in the information section of the Annual Guide to the Canadian Classification and Dictionary of Occupants, put out by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), that within the next few years a series of books will be replacing the present CCD volume, and the first book in this series, "Construction Occupations", is being published under separate cover. I assumed this study is in connection with the production of this particular book.
I wondered what would be produced because in looking at the document to which I have already referred, I saw something I found interesting under "Tree Trimmer". It tells me that a tree trimmer trims trees, climbs trees, prunes tree tops and branches, using saws and pruning shears. He trims damaged trees and paints stumps. He removes broken limbs and he fells trees. Then in relation to occasional duties it says that he works from a bucket on an extended truck boom to reach the branches. If that is the kind of information that is considered confidential, then the House will understand why I suggest that these documents should be produced.
Looking at this book, quite by coincidence 1 noted that under "Cook (cater, and lodg.)"-that is, catering and lodging, the first item-there are 38 different kinds of cooks, including everything from catering and lodging down to the

March 1, 1979
Job Studies
thirty-eighth "cook, vacuum kettle"; but nowhere in the list does it mention a plain, ordinary cook. I inquired and found out that they are going to correct this deficiency, and I shall be able soon to tell my wife what is a plain, ordinary cook.
Just to continue in this same vein-and maybe I am being a little lighthearted this afternoon-under "Hair-curler maker" we find five groupings down to "hair stylist", but it does not mention hair grooming.
Another interesting one covers everything from aquarium attendant down to an aquatic-biology technologist; but I find they have forgotten aquacultural technician. Hon. members can understand why I was interested in seeing what they were going to produce for the construction industry.
My interests stems-and now I am going to be serious for a moment-from the fact that most of us, whether we are federal members of parliament or otherwise, look upon construction generally as being a provincial area of responsibility. I wonder why the federal government should be mixing into what is generally accepted as provincial jurisdiction.
To get back to something a little lighter, I notice in this book a "guide to qualifications profile factors", something which I presume is used in categorizing these various groupings. I find a very interesting group referred to as "physical activities". I mention this because it could be of interest to members of parliament in that it groups various workers in categories of sedentary work, light work, medium work, heavy work and very heavy work. 1 presume that we as members of parliament are in the sedentary work category. We are permitted to lift, carry, push or pull up to 10 pounds but no more. We also see in this same list reference to climbing and/or balancing, stooping, kneeling, crouching and/or crawling, reaching, handling, fingering and/or feeling, talking, hearing and seeing in various terms, and control of the hand and control of the foot. I think we should put all members of parliament through this questionnaire.
To be serious, Mr. Speaker, there are many questions I want to ask about this study which might have been answered had I been able to get my hands on these papers. Obviously I want to ask why the study was considered necessary, how often such a study is done, and I would like to know how up-to-date it is to be kept. I would like to know who uses this Canadian Classification and Dictionary of Occupants, and who in construction trades is going to use the book when it is put out. I would like to know how many are going to be printed, how many are going to be distributed and to whom they are going to be distributed. I would like to know how they are going to be used by other departments and whether other departments of governments are really interested in construction workers.
I should also like to know why Southam Business Publications was picked. I am not objecting at the moment, but I would like to know if there was a tender call. I would like to know what price was paid in terms of this reference, and I would like to know why 1,600 was the figure adopted. I would like to know who decided on 1,600. I assume it was the Department of Employment and Immigration, but why 1,600, and what kinds of jobs were the 1,600 to cover? Was it all

trades in the construction industry? How many in each province? Are we comparing the differences from province to province? Did the provinces agree and co-operate? Was every trade covered in every province? Because as everyone knows, each province handles the construction industry differently. I wonder if apprentices were covered. Apprenticeship is quite an issue at the present, particularly in the province of Quebec.
If I might interject a point of some concern here, it is that the control of apprenticeships is also affecting the number of persons in a particular trade which can enter into the work force. Obviously, one way of controlling the supply of that type of labour is to control those who are entering at the bottom, the apprentices. Another important point is that since the provinces are responsibles and since they set up the apprenticeship centres, the provinces can also control the language used, and this has become quite a factor to persons who wish to enter into the construction industry but are barred because of language restrictions.
I wonder if in this study the apprenticeship levels of competence were considered from province to province. Once again, because it is a provincial concern the different provinces make their own decisions as to the number of years of apprenticeship required in each particular trade. I do not know the situation in each province, having only been a member of parliament for some seven years now, but with regard to Quebec I wonder if the persons who were being considered were all holding competency cards and if the problem of issuance of competency cards was dealt with in the study.
Was a study made of the comparison of union and nonunion construction workers in those provinces which are not fully unionized? Was any comparison made of the differences in qualifications between a unionized carpenter and a nonunionized carpenter? Also, did they consider self-employed construction workers? I mention self-employed construction workers because it is my experience that the productivity of this type of worker is similar to the productivity of the self-employed construction worker of some 25 years ago, whereas the production of the regular construction worker, unionized or non-unionized, is considerably less than what it was 25 years ago. This is one of the reasons field construction today is so much more expensive and why there is less field construction going on than there is factory construction.
! find it quite extraordinary that this situation has developed to the point where a factory-made house today, for example, can be produced at about half the price of a field constructed house. I do not wish to get into the bill which is presently being discussed in the House, but it is apropos to my motion when discussing the construction worker who works in the factory and who is generally considered unskilled as compared to the man who is working in the field doing almost the same job. I wonder if this has been taken into account. In other words, a man operating a gun which shoots nails into plywood and who works for a factory is probably not considered in this study as
March 1, 1979

being in the same grouping as the construction worker in the field who uses a hammer to beat nails into plywood.
I wonder if the problems of these overlapping responsibilities which often result in union disputes were a consideration. Quite obviously, the union worker is finding that there is less work available to him because of the increase in the amount of work which is taking the form of factory production today. From a construction point of view this is easily understood. To illustrate, three weeks ago I visited a factory that produces prefabricated houses. These are houses of which all of us could be proud, containing three bedrooms, a fully equipped kitchen, carpeting, hardwood floors, tiles, all that one would expect in a nice house. The opposition may also be interested to know that these houses are being sold in the province of Quebec on a serviced lot for a total cost of $32,000.
I wonder how these people who conducted the study looked at the limits of a particular trade. I wonder if they concerned themselves with the different wage rates that pertain par-ticuarly in areas where there are union and non-union workers working side by side. Most of all, however, I am concerned about the apparent interference-and I would like this explained-of the federal government in what I consider to be an area of provincial jurisdiction.
That is why I ask for these papers. The federal government is studying these construction trades and considers that it has the right to do so, whereas it stated categorically that it would not express similar interest in education. I am inclined to the view that if we are going to mix in provincial responsibilities, perhaps education would be a good place to start.
I have one last point which I consider of major importance with regard to the province of Quebec. Since the study was authorized by the Department of Employment and Immigration, I wonder what their attitude is with regard to the use of hiring halls in the province of Quebec and the fact that the construction companies are not able to go to the Ministry of Employment and Immigration for the labour which they require. In fact, the Department of Employment and Immigration has been effectively shut out in the province of Quebec. I am not saying that this is wrong; I am only pointing out that in Quebec the Department of Employment and Immigration can have very little interest in the employment of construction workers because the hiring is done through the hiring halls.
Lastly, Mr. Speaker, though I have been somewhat lighthearted in my approach to this particular motion and though I have no doubt that the government will continue to refuse to produce these papers which I consider are of relatively little importance to them, my chief concern in bringing this matter forward for debate is this apparent interference in an area of provincial jurisdiction. I have asked a great deal of questions and hopefully the parliamentary secretary will have noted some of them and will be able to refer some answers back to me.

Mr. Speaker, my intervention will not be very long. I would like to thank the hon. member for introducing this motion. It just goes to show
Job Studies
one why it is so important to have leadership, as has been provided by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), in the area of freedom of information.
As I understand it, this government is committed to this sort of thing, yet I hear the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) blasting the parliamentary secretary because that hon. member says the type of information that is required is confidential. Even though his remarks were lighthearted, I think that was an attempt to cover his anger at what the parliamentary secretary was doing.
He says he wants to see jobs studies in the construction industry. He should understand that the construction industry is one of the most important in this country. I do not intend to get involved with provincial jurisdiction as my hon. friend did; he has researched it and I have not. One of the main problems with this industry at the moment is the lack of work. There is no industrial strategy which would create a climate of confidence and put people to work.
Between 1977 and 1978 there was a decline in construction employment. In 1978 the average unemployment rate in the construction industry in Newfoundland was 31 per cent, in Nova Scotia, 22 per cent, in New Brunswick, 23 per cent, in Quebec, 20 per cent, in Ontario, 12 per cent, in Manitoba, 12 per cent, in Saskatchewan, 11 per cent, in Alberta, 7 per cent, and in British Columbia, 13 per cent. Only in Alberta was the unemployment rate down.
It is significant that these figures do not show that there is a very high rate of unemployment within the trade union movement. Within this very vital and important industry there is a skill bank and we are not making sufficient withdrawal from it. 1 do not really want to blame the federal government but the fact is that they have no industrial strategy. There is no climate of confidence and consequently we find ourselves in a mess.
Another factor is the mobility of construction workers. I understand that the Department of Employment and Immigration has appointed a task force to look into this matter. I am given to understand that there are about 4,000 unemployed carpenters in British Columbia, though there is a shortage of carpenters in Calgary where business is apparently booming. This is the sort of thing we want to know. We want the information set out in these 1,600 job studies, some of which concern the construction trade. This is the sort of thing we need in order to cope with this enormous problem.
The president of the Hamilton Construction Association has indicated that there is nothing in Hamilton to sustain the industry after this year. Surely if this is to be a viable industry, one that can make a significant contribution toward a greater industrial nation, then the type of question that the hon. member has placed on the order paper must be answered. I will be very interested to see if the parliamentary secretary flim-flams and tries to justify refusing this information.
It is our position that the onus is upon the government to show why the information cannot be released. I think most

March 1, 1979
Job Studies
information can be released unless it is in the line of security. On a simple question pertaining to job studies it makes no sense to be told that the information is confidential. I believe this is doing irreparable harm and is unwarranted. If a climate of activity and excitement is to be created in the construction industry, surely the information required to do this could be made available.
With these few remarks, Mr. Speaker, I want to let the parliamentary secretary know that, in my opinion, the construction industry is one of the vital industries in this country and every effort should be made to create a climate of confidence in it. This refusal on the part of the parliamentary secretary-whether the one who is going to speak now or his predecessor-was irresponsible and shortsighted. He has tunnel vision. I hope I am not directing my remarks to the parliamentary secretary who is going to stand up now. If I am, I do not mean in the way it sounds, and I will withdraw most of it. He will have to figure out which part.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the desire of the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) to get the documents to which he was refused access. I do so because we on this side of the House have had this experience on many occasions. It is good to know, although not very helpful, that we are not alone and that the government treats its own members in the same cavalier manner as it treats us.
It is part of the madness of this government that it refuses to give information to the public, members of parliament, the media and educators-information which is of the utmost importance if the problems which this country faces are to be dealt with in a rational manner and solved.
This government, which has been in power for 55 of the last 65 years, has come to believe it has all the answers and can refuse to give the most elementary and necessary information to anybody and everybody.
I have no knowledge of the study dealing with problems in the construction industry which the hon. member for Vaudreuil wanted. I have a copy, however, of a study made for the Department of Manpower and Immigration by Robertson, Nickerson, Group Associates Ltd., entitled "Case Studies in Aspects of Training Upper Skilled Blue Collar Workers". This is a study of the problems and needs in the manufacturing industry which is probably complementary to the study which the hon. member for Vaudreuil would like dealing with the construction industry.
Any minister or deputy minister who has read this report should hang his head in shame-if he did not immediately offer his resignation. The study shows that the opportunity for high level young Canadians to enter a skilled trade is so remote as to be described as non-existent. It points out that there is a shortage of upper skilled workers now and that the shortage will get more serious as the economy picks up. It also says that industrial growth in Canada will be inhibited by a lack of skilled workers. According to this study, government programs are not receiving industry support and need a mas-

sive overhaul. This refers to a department of government which has spent $2.5 billion on job training in the last five years. Last year we spent $680 million on the job training. Of that amount only $80 million went to subsidize on the job training, namely training in industry, in companies involved in manufacturing. The provincial educational institutions received $340 million, and $260 million was paid directly to individuals for income support while attending provincial technical schools.
We spent $2'/2 billion in the last five years and we still have a million unemployed. What did this group hired by the department to look into the situation in the manufacturing industries have to say? They said there is a crying need for skilled people.
Since World War II most of our needs for skilled workers have been met by immigrants. We have imported the people we needed. Because of high unemployment in Canada, one million unemployed, naturally Canadians are saying to government that we have to cut back on the number of immigrants we permit to come into this country. One cannot blame the people of Canada when they see one million unemployed. That is why they do not want more people coming here. The government has responded to that feeling. Last year it cut back substantially on the number of immigrants permitted to come to this country.
At the same time as we are wanting to cut back because we have unemployment, skilled workers who could come to this country if there were jobs available are not coming because unemployment in the industrialized countries, particularly in western Europe, is much lower than it is here. Their standard of living has risen compared to the standard of living in Canada.
A few years ago the average per capita income of Canadian citizens was the second highest in the world. We were second to the United States. Today, we are seventh or eighth. West Germany, Sweden, Norway and Denmark, just to mention a few, have all gone ahead of us. The result is that the skilled immigrants we attracted in the years after World War II no longer want to come to this country. That is the situation.
As the report to which I referred indicates, there is a grim shortage of skilled tradesmen. The report indicates a tremendous shortage of tool and die makers, machinists, and electronic technicians. They are and will be needed in large numbers all across the country. They will particularly be needed if this or whatever government is in power in the next few years can get the economy moving, and instead of having 83 per cent of our capacity being used we will use 90 or 93 per cent, which is what it should be. The shortage of skilled workers in Canada would then cause a real crisis situation. That shortage has been attested to by companies all across the country. The shortage in the manufacturing industry which I talked about is just as prevalent in the construction industry about which the hon. member for Vaudreuil was asking.
March 1, 1979

Something that everyone but the manpower department is agreed on is that our manpower training programs are tragically inadequate. They are a disaster. There are reasons for that, such as jurisdictional disputes between Ottawa and the provinces. Under the provisions of the British North America Act, the provinces have responsibility for education. The federal government has taken the responsibility for manpower training.
I believe, and I have expressed this view since the day the Department of Manpower was set up, that the division which the federal government insisted on between manpower training and education is an artificial division. It does not work in practice. The federal government has insisted on its jurisdiction. It has designed manpower programs to a large extent in a vacuum, without consultation with the provinces, industry and the unions. The result is what we predicted. When I have more time I will prove, by quotations and illustrations from industries and corporations, the kinds of shortages which I have indicated.
We have spent tremendous amounts of money, but we have no reliable information about our future needs in the construction industry, the manufacturing industry, and the service field. There are very few really good training programs on the job in the plants. Most of the money is spent in institutions which were built with the financial carrot of federal funding for construction and operations held before them.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the Chair would explain to me what connection the hon. member's remarks have with the motion we are discussing here this afternoon.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member should listen to the speech and not ask the Chair to explain to him what the hon. member is saying.

Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member would listen he would understand, which 1 doubt he has the intelligence to do from listening to his many interjections. He would know that I am supporting the request of the hon. member for Vaudreuil for documents pertaining to studies on manpower needs in the construction industry. I am doing that by summarizing a similar need for documents with regard to manpower needs in the manufacturing industry. There is a close relationship between what I am saying and what was said by the hon. member for Vaudreuil.
I was saying, before I was somewhat rudely interrupted, that there are very few good on the job training programs in industry. Where there are such programs, too few apprentices are being trained. The reason for that is that it is cheaper for employers to take the easy way out when they need skilled workers. They either depend on the educational system, which we now know has failed miserably, or they recruit immigrants.
There is no quick or easy solution to the problems we face. We need programs to meet both the short and long-term needs. The federal government should stop trying to make all decisions unilaterally as it has been doing since the manpower
Job Studies
department was set up. We must stop turning the tap off and on by contracting for more or less seats in the community colleges. Decisions as to how many seats to purchase in our community colleges are not based on the needs of the region or the country, but on political and budgetary considerations. In this period of restraint we should at least partially turn off the tap because we do not have the money. In a period in which we think we need to prime the pump, we turn the tap on.
The federal government, the provinces, industry and labour must get together to work out programs to meet our needs. The one body which could secure that collaboration and co-ordination is the federal government, though it has not shown any inclination to do so up until now. The federal government should invite provinces, industry and labour to assess the need and, upon the basis of that assessment, to develop the necessary programs. But this cannot be done because nobody, except possibly the federal government, knows what the needs are. The only information available is in the possession of the federal government which refuses to give it to the hon. member for Vaudreuil, to other members on this side, to industry, labour, or anyone else.
I join with the hon. member for Vaudreuil in urging the government and the Department of Manpower to change its policy, its desire to keep everything secret. I urge the government to make available as much information as possible so that the people as individuals and through their organizations, whether trade unions or companies or manufacturers' associations, can really begin thinking about the problems we face and attempting to find solutions to them.

speakeroldname: Mr. Frank Maine (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in responding to the request of the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) for the tabling in the House of approximately 1,600 job studies in the construction trades series which were prepared in order to update the Canadian Classification and Dictionary of Occupations (CCDO), and were carried out under contract by Southam Business Publications, Don Mills, Ontario, I am bound to say there is a very compelling reason why I cannot agree to that motion.
In many instances job information collected for studies such as these is considered to be confidential by the companies concerned. As a result, to reassure those establishment assisting in this program, the then Department of Manpower and Immigration gave an undertaking that the information supplied by companies would be treated as strictly confidential. Under the circumstances the tabling of these job studies in the House would constitute a breach of trust on the part of the government and I cannot condone such a course of action.
I am sure that my hon. friend from Vaudreuil knows that during the past two decades Canada has experienced a period of rapid economic development. The growth of a technological society produces numerous socio-economic changes. Although each economy makes similar responses to technological change, its job structures are largely a reflection of its own

March 1, 1979
Job Studies
policies, developments and goals. For this reason it is desirable to establish and maintain an occupational classification system suited to its national requirements.
A multi-purpose standard classification of occupations is an important instrument for studying the development and utilization of employment resources. It needs to be standardized because, for research and analysis purposes, data compiled on the basis of one system cannot be compared satisfactorily with data compiled on the basis of other systems. It needs to be multi-purpose because standardization is worthless unless it meets the needs of various users and facilitates communications between them.
Experience has shown that the development of a standard occupational classification which completely satisfies the requirements of every probable user may not be possible but one that services as many needs as possible is invaluable. Statisticians or economists studying the labour force are normally concerned with wide groups of jobs rather than individual jobs. Their statistics are usually assembled in a limited number of categories designed to contain job groupings which are relatively homogeneous in terms of a particular characteristic. On the other hand, continuing labour market programs such as job placement, vocational counselling, training and immigration deal with individuals, and thus specific occupational definitions are needed. For statistical reporting purposes, however, the latter programs are also concerned with wider groups of related jobs. This common interest provides a link between persons concerned with otherwise different programs.
The concept of a standardized occupational coding system has been recognized by many countries as essential for effective labour market planning, employment operations and career development. In October, 1966, the Quadrennial Conference of Labour Statisticians at Geneva endorsed the concept of national multi-purpose classification systems and urged that these systems be related to the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO).
Because Canada did not then have its own standard occupational classification system, a number of quite different systems had been used for many years. Statistics Canada used a classification system suitable for collecting and compiling information from census enumerations, but not for other purposes. The job placement operations of Canada Manpower Centres used the United States Dictionary of Occupational Titles (DOT) to code occupations, while the immigration service, for a number of years, used the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO). It was difficult to compare data compiled from one system with data compiled from the other two systems. The use of a variety of systems tended to complicate planning and operational activities.
Social scientists require an occupational classification system that enables them to determine the actual changes which have taken place in the structure of the labour force. Such a system is essential for analytical studies and the preparation of projections and forecasts. The design of a Canadian classification system had to ensure, as much as

possible, the historical continuity of statistical data. Statistics Canada, therefore, had considerable interest in and input into the initial design of an occupational classification system that was to be convertible to, and a replacement for, the 1961 Canada Census and compatible with the revised International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO) for international study and report purposes. The then Department of Manpower and Immigration required a system that was convertible to the American Dictionary of Occupational Titles (DOT) because past records were coded to this system. In 1966, to resolve these inadequacies, the Department of Manpower and Immigration and Statistics Canada launched a joint project to develop a standard national classification.
The main objective of the Canadian Classification and Dictionary of Occupations, or CCDO as it is familiarly known, is to provide for Canada a standard multi-purpose instrument for use in labour market research and analysis, for statistical survey purposes including census taking, and for operational activities such as placement, counselling, training and immigration. It is designed to facilitate analysis in various manpower fields, for example, job market analysis and worker mobility; it is a useful tool in career counselling and placement services; it provides essential data for the planning and evaluation of educational and training programs; and it has many uses for personnel operations in business and industry.
The census occupational classification which is now based on the Canadian Classification and Dictionary of Occupations is widely used throughout Canada in many statistical surveys. Thus, the CCDO has achieved the most important function of a multi-purpose classification system, for example, increasing the quantity and improving the quality of occupational information in Canada by standardizing the occupational categories and definitions used in different programs and, consequently, the occupational statistics and other information derived from various sources.
Internationally, CCDO is recognized as the leader in systems of this kind. In such diverse countries as Japan, Mexico, Algeria and Fiji, CCDO has had a direct influence on the development of national systems. Recently, after having reviewed the major systems available, Australia has opted to base its own system on the CCDO approach and has asked the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission for assistance. The United States, which is only now moving toward a system comparable to Canada's, recently published the "Standard Occupational Classification Manual", and in the foreword it says:
In its work, the project staff also considered new developments on occupational classification at the international level. In this regard, the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO), the Canadian Classification and Dictionary of Occupations, and the British Classification of Occupations and Directory of Occupational Titles were major references.
Extensive use was made of the Canadian Classification; we are grateful to the Canadian government for their permission to use concept, definitions, and phrases from their publications in this classification.
March 1, 1979

Canada's lead in this field is being maintained and expanded as the system adjusts itself to face an automated future. This lead and excellence could well be jeopardized if we dried up the sources of valuable detailed data volunteered to us under the protection of confidentiality.
The actual nature of work performed was selected as the basic principle in the CCDO because it is significant to all users of the multi-purpose classification system. Other criteria such as "training time required" or "working environment" were considered and rejected. Such criteria are related more closely to the worker than to the occupation and are thus more subjective in character. For this reason they are not acceptable as basic criteria to all users of a multi-purpose classification structure.
The CCDO classification is a coded taxonomic structure that organizes occupations into distinct categories. The first category consists of 23 major groups which describe broad fields of work. The second category consists of 81 minor groups which are further subdivisions of related fields of work. The third category consists of 498 unit groups which describe closely related groups of occupations. These three categories permit the aggregation of statistics at three different levels and are designed for the common statistical reporting requirements of all types of programs dealing with occupations. Within each of the three category or unit groups we find several individually coded and defined related occupations. This latter development serves the needs of job placement, immigration, counselling and training.
The important basic principle of using "work performed" to develop categories at all levels in the CCDO was determined by the duties and tasks indicated by job analyses conducted in private and public establishments and institutions, and through a variety of associations across Canada. In order to gain the co-operation of these establishments and institutions it was First necessary, as I have already mentioned, to give an undertaking on behalf of the federal government that all data gathered by our analysts would not be directly linked to the establishments which co-operated. If these 1,600 studies were tabled in this House, this undertaking would be severely shaken and I am, therefore, opposed to the tabling of these studies.

Mr. Speaker, it was not over a month ago that I stood in my place and supported the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), who was then seeking information on an entirely different subject. At that time I sat and thought perhaps there was something very secret in what he was seeking. I thought that again today. I thought perhaps there is something which should not be made public. However, the situation is the same now as it was then. What we got again today was gobbledygook, bafflegab and flimflam.
I have to say that the parliamentary secretary reads exceptionally well. I do not know that in 12 or 14 minutes I could handle all those 35-cent words one after the other. It used to be that they were 25-cent words, but this government has pushed inflation so high that those words now cost 35 cents.
Job Studies
I have never heard such nonsense in all my life. No one expects the government to make known in this House the fact that John Jones is working for the Dow Construction Company or what he does. That is not the point. We are not in the least interested in that. I have spent all my life in construction. I am not directly involved now to the extent I was years ago, but I am still involved in construction in a peripheral way, and I know that the information which has been discussed would be very valuable.
I commend the hon. member for Vaudreuil. As the hon. member ticked questions off his list, I thought to myself that that information would be worthwhile to a contractor or a construction man. I do not care whether Mr. Jones works for Dow Construction, but I would like to see the results of all this study. I would like to know the answers to the hon. member's questions. If the Department of Employment and Immigration received answers, it should give us those answers. We are not interested in names. We do not need to know that a job on the corner of Gladstone Avenue and Bank Street was done in a certain way. We do not need to know that, but if the department got answers to all those questions, why in heaven's name can we not have them?
Surely in our enlightened age we know that if the government gets information from certain contractors, it will not pass it on to another contractor to help him bid in opposition. I cannot believe that as he stood in his place the parliamentary secretary believed that nonsense. However, he stood there for 12 minutes. He spewed out words about CCDO, ISCO and all kinds of things. He has not the foggiest notion of what they mean. I have a great deal of respect for my friend from the Wellington area. He is an excellent scientist, but I would bet that he has never done a bit of construction work in his life. If he had, he would realize the value of this information. He would realize that the possession of this information by contractors would produce tremendous results.
I know this government gets involved in this sort of thing. In the last few days we have seen some indications of what the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mrs. Cam-pagnolo) and her department can do with computers. The Department of Public Works has a computer specification coming out, and it is a dandy. By golly, you can push a button and get a 15-page specification for a push-button on an outhouse door. However, if we are going to do all of this and if we are going to put all this information into a computer, why can we not get it out?
Why did the hon. member for Vaudreuil not receive an answer to his question? He is not asking for names or details. I did not count them, but I think there were 25 or 30 questions, all of them legitimate questions. Let us see if we cannot get the answers. They would be valuable to the whole of the construction industry. Surely to goodness there is no justification for hiding the answers, unless it is the innate sense of secrecy of this government.

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised that hon. members opposite, with the exception of the last speaker, should get up and demand

March 1, 1979
Housing
information without knowing what they are talking about. They are asking that the government release information it promised industry it would keep confidential. It surprises me even more to hear an experienced member like the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) talk for ten or 15 minutes all around the subject but refer to it directly only at the opening and closing of his remarks. The hon. member for Winnipeg North spoke about something else and pretended that what was at issue was a report instead of the date on which the report is based. The hon. member was being either devious or dumb, and the House can be the arbiter of that question.
There is a vast amount of information here. The opposition is always complaining about the government's wasting taxpayers' money, but on the other hand it says it would spend more. Now hon. members opposite want somebody in the employ of the public to go through the interviews upon which these 1,600 job classifications were based, remove all names or references to companies or individuals, and then table all that information in the House.
Who would use it? Certainly not the hon. members we have heard from today.

Mr. Speaker, before we moved on to other business at five o'clock I was speaking on the housing bill before us today and the criticisms I have of it in terms of the Liberal government moving away from an activist role to the degree that is needed for providing afford-

able housing to Canadians. I began analysing what were the reasons behind the high cost of housing and I elaborated on the fact that the cost of materials is increasing, the cost of labour is increasing, and the interest rate on mortgages is going up. The fourth factor on which I should like to comment is that what is pushing up the cost of housing is the cost of land. It is only by understanding what the causes are that we can hope to come up with solutions to the problems.
The cost of land in Canada for housing has been rising at astronomical rates over the past few years. One study shows that the cost of lots in any moderate-sized community from 1971 onward at least has doubled, and in some cases has moved higher in price than that. Of course there are a number of developers assembling land in urban areas. They are sitting on that land, holding on to it, and allowing the price to increase through speculation and lack of supply. They only release a certain amount of land at a time. Also studies have shown the control of land in major urban centres is in the hands of a very small number of developers.
What has happened is that we do not have much competition any longer in terms of land development. Certainly this is no exception in my community of Sault Ste. Marie. Indeed certain prominent members of the Conservative party are involved very heavily in land assembly in the Sault Ste. Marie area.
One study shows just what is happening with land developers. Profits gained by large suburban land developers have added some $7,000 to $10,000 to the price of new $50,000 homes in cities such as Regina and Winnipeg. In Ontario, the Peel Housing Task Force found that profits on lots were 22 per cent of the final selling price of houses. One can only conclude that certain developers are making windfall profits, and that is a major factor in forcing up the cost of housing.
Of all the reasons I have given for the increase in the cost of housing, I think two stand out above all others, namely, the cost of land and the cost of mortgage interest rates. If we are to have any kind of meaningful government policy to deal with rising prices in housing, we must tackle those two key problems, the cost of money and the cost of land. Throughout the history of housing policy of the Liberal government, and even its Conservative predecessor, we do not find any policy or legislation addressing itself to those key problems.
I do not think we would find much initiative on the part of the Liberal government, or for that matter a Conservative government, in terms of attacking the banks and telling them they must bring down their interest rates for certain income groups. There is a very cozy relationship between the two old line parties and the Canadian banking institution. I was interested in reading the reports of the 1977 Election Expenses Act which listed the contributions political parties received from various sectors and interest groups. What caught my eye was the amount of money donated by Canadian banks to the Liberal and Conservative parties.
March 1, 1979

For example, in 1977, according to the official returns, the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce donated $25,000 to the Liberal party and $25,195 to the Conservative party. The Bank of Nova Scotia gave the Liberals $21,500 and the Conservatives $20,000. The list goes on and on. There is a rather vested interest on the part of the old line parties and the banks which charge these interest rates. I would be very surprised to see any kind of meaningful government initiative to attack such generous donators to its political causes.
In terms of dealing with the horrendously high cost of mortgage interest rates, one must recall that over a period of a 25-year mortgage in the amount of $40,000, with an interest rate of 10 per cent, $4,000 a year is paid in interest alone. That is forgetting about even reducing the principal amount borrowed. Over the term of a 25-year mortgage, a $40,000 or $50,000 house costs in excess of $100,000, and of course the great bulk of it is interest charges.
We in the New Democratic Party say that the only way to attack that major contributor to rising costs of housing is for the government to become tough with the banks and to say to the lending institutions, which have been making incredible profits over the past few years, that they can afford to absorb a less high profit by reducing or offering 8 per cent mortgages to families earning $25,000 or less. There are ways and means by which the government, through the Bank of Canada, could direct the lending institutions to make such lower cost mortgages available to Canadians who want to own homes. Of course this would help renters, the majority of our people who live in apartments. It would provide them with an opportunity to own homes, the dream of many couples. Especially it would help young couples who must face mortgage payments of $400 a month under the present situation. It would bring down dramatically the monthly mortgage bill if 8 per cent mortgages were available. Surely that is a much more progressive means of dealing with high interest rates than any of the proposals I have heard from either of the old line parties.
The only way we can deal with the high cost of land is by the implementation of certain taxation legislation to make it very unattractive for land speculation on the part of developers. It would be more important to move into the idea of public land banking by municipal or provincial governments assembling land which will be released when needed, at prices people can afford, rather than it being left in private hands and suffering the price escalation I have described.
Government funding for low rental housing and senior citizens' units must be enhanced and increased. As I said earlier, I am dismayed the government is pulling back and not offering the needed funds for this very worth-while housing.
In the course of my speech I would be remiss if I did not examine with some seriousness the proposal of the official opposition, the Conservative party, offering a mortgage interest deduction up to a total of $5,000 and a property tax deduction up to $1,000 as a solution to the high cost of housing. I can only conclude that it is a pre-election gimmick on the part of the Conservative party. Every study I have seen shows that it would be just too costly to implement such a
Housing
program, that it would cost Canadian taxpayers $2 billion to $3 billion a year in lost revenue, which would only increase the deficit.
It is ironic that the Conservative party, which daily attacks the Liberal government for a huge deficit, would advocate a policy to increase the deficit even more. If members of the Conservative party argue its proposal will not increase the deficit, the only way it would do so is if taxpayers pay for it in terms of higher taxes in order to make up the lost revenue through the mortgage and property tax deduction scheme. If we did not take that course in raising taxes to put this scheme in place, then the only other course would be to reduce government services which are now in place further, and in that way reduce spending. Of course, that would only make those who need these vital government programs suffer from the lack of them. I think this is a gimmick and I hope Canadians are not taken in by it. As I said, we can not afford it.
There is a built-in unfairness to this program because it does nothing for tenants. About one third of all households in Canada are described as renters and they would get absolutely no tax benefit from this home owner interest deduction scheme. Nor, of course, would senior citizens, who probably have paid for their houses and are not holding active mortgages. This is unfair as well because it would probably mean interest rates would rise as there would be a greater demand for mortgage funds. More people would probably re-mortgage their homes in order to obtain the advantages of the tax break. In addition, the interest rate could be written off against taxes and there would be no pressure, and there is little now, to keep interest rates down. I imagine the banks would seize the opportunity of increasing mortgage rates even more.
The major default in terms of unfairness in the program is, of course, that it benefits upper income Canadians more than middle or low income Canadians. Surely we do not need any more inequities built into our present tax system than are already there, courtesy of a decade of the Trudeau Liberal policy.
When we look at the inspiration for this mortgage deducta-bility scheme we see it comes from the United States which has a plan already in place. Most United States housing experts, and many government officials, would like to get out of that program because it costs so much and because, as I say, it is so unfair.
The U.S. Treasury Department conducted a study in 1977 of this program which the Conservatives want to bring into Canada and discovered that the highest income group, that is to say, 15 per cent of U.S. taxpayers, derive 75 per cent of the benefits from the plan. It works in such a way that the more you make and the higher your mortgage payments, the more of a deduction you get from your taxes.
What would happen in Canada is that middle income taxpayers would save a couple of hundred dollars under the Conservative plan, but someone in the top bracket would get a

March 1, 1979
Housing
windfall of $4,000 when calculating taxes in the way that this system operates.
Surely if any party in this House, particularly the federal Conservative party, is concerned about a fair tax system, it should follow the Conservative counterpart in the province of Ontario. That government does not have a tax deduction system but a tax credit system for home owners and tenants. The advantage of a tax credit system is that it is on a lower income scale and is cut off at the upper income level. The tax credit system has fairness built into it, and statistics show that the greatest benefits go to the lower and middle income wage earners.
Under the present scheme with the federal Conservative plan, the greatest benefit would go to upper income Canadians and not to those who need them the most. In other words, the Tory philosophy is, the more you earn the less taxes you should pay. I think any honest political party would reject that as a proper base for a tax system. What we have in terms of the old line parties is a gimmick by the Conservatives, and general indifference by the Liberals, when it comes to implementing a viable housing policy for Canadians, especially designed to get at the two key problems, high mortgage rates and high cost of land.
The policies that my party has outlined during the debate, and elsewhere, on the whole issue of bringing interest rates down and the cost of land down, make more sense and offer much more hope to tenants, young couples and others who desperately want and need affordable housing. This is the direction in which we should be moving, not in the direction that this bill proposes, or in the direction of the gimmickers of the Conservative party.

Mr. Speaker, I hope that the opposition party will soon put an end to their foolish tricks to delay the proceedings in the House and will finally let us speak once and for all. I am therefore pleased to speak once again in the House, especially about Bill C-29 on housing. Since I have been sitting in the House, I have always been hoping for a housing policy governing corporations and nonprofit housing co-operatives. So I am quite pleased to see that

we are now considering amendments to the legislation which will allow us to fill some gaps and make improvements.
First, Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate and thank the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) for having agreed to introduce this bill in parliament and 1 hope it will be passed before the next election. And before going further I have a short message to give to the Progressive Conservative party. They will probably be disappointed but I must say to them that I will be a candidate in the next election. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that this legislation will fill some gaps.
There are experiences that have been lived through. I remember that before I was elected to Parliament, when I was with the Workmen's Compensation Board, I used to take mornings or afternoons off to go to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to try to do something because in the district where I come from, in Hochelaga-Maisonneuve, Ste. Marie, St. Jacques, La Salle or even in Verdun, there certainly is a housing problem, it is obvious. Being conscious of these problems, like any good citizen having lived in slums, having lived what the people are living today, I thought I must do something.

Of course, we were thinking of senior citizens, families, we wanted to develop low rental housing, but at the time that was not possible, because things were going too slow. It took at least two years to build a unit.
Two out of six units were occupied during a period of a year and a half. Why? Because costs were too high and because of

the slowness not only of CMEIC, but also of the city of Montreal, because there are regulations, the National Building Code, the Municipal Building Code, all of which create confusion and slow things down. Building costs increase and in the end, what can we offer people? Not low rental housing, but high price housing.
Naturally, I do not blame the minister for that. Nor do I blame the National Elousing Act: it is just there. But what happens too often is that those who administer the act are obsessed with setting up regulations that often run counter to our wishes as legislators, I feel we must some day find a way, when we pass a law, not to be exposed to being laughed at later on by the people or the civil servants who say: Sure, you are the legislators but come the next election and you may no longer be there while we will still be here. Those are the answers we get, Mr. Speaker. But it does not matter, these people need not worry because after the next election we will still be here on this side of the House. That I can guarantee.
Hear, hear!

Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to address myself to a certain point and I will do so briefly, of course. We know that the National Housing Act allows any home owner to apply for a grant to repair his house. So what happens in my riding and obviously in others is that people go to Montreal, more particularly on St. Paul Street, to apply for grants and are told: "Sure you will get a grant, but it will take a year and a half before you are paid". Considering that everyone in my constituency is not a millionaire, people get discouraged and forget about the grant. Meanwhile the whole neighbourhood is deteriorating. I invite any of my colleagues from this House who are interested to come and spend one day in the riding of Hochelaga, in Maisonneuve or in Sainte-Marie to visit one street after another. We see more and more derelict houses. What happens then? We all know that a number of aged people live in slums although their pension is reasonable. But it turns out to be expensive for people living in slums. Indeed, medicare is higher because people get sick, heat is higher and so on and so forth. If those who were here before us in this House as well as in Quebec City and in Montreal had thought of the future we would certainly not have ended up with a situation where neighbourhoods like ours are disappearing. And I think that in the case of a ward like mine everything should be undertaken to protect it, not to protect it in a narrow sense but to revive it and keep the traditional image which it has always had and to give its inhabitants decent houses. I suggest that in this society which claims to be just and civilized, we should be able to demand from our governments decent housing and security for our people. I suggest also that if we fail to do so, we should not go and say to the faces of Canadians that we are civilized people, for I should be the first to deny it and say that on the contrary we are heartless people who do not care for our senior citizens.

Mr. Speaker, let us take the case of the low rent housing situation in Montreal. Last year the city of Montreal had a supply of 600 housing units to meet the demand of some 6,000 applicants. This supply represented only 10 per cent of the demand. 1 feel therefore that all interested parties should join hands to increase the number of units, and I am sure that some members in the opposition are afraid this bill will cost too much. Well, I have news for them. I shall not go into details, that would be too simple, Mr. Speaker; if they do not understand them, I hope the voters will take advantage of the forthcoming election to send them packing. It is not complicated. Mr. Speaker, when amounts of money are invested in non-profit corporations or co-ops, it is clear that after 25, 30, 40 or 50 years, they will say: "So what! In 30 years, the hon. member for Hochelaga will not be here any longer". It is true he will no longer be here. As a matter of fact, it is quite certain. But today, he is here. He is here to pave the way, like his hon. colleagues. That is what we are going to do, Mr. Speaker.
And you will see that all the figures which the opposition can produce are wrong, because we will invest in housing; after 30, 35 or 50 years non-profit corporations can make no profit whatsoever, and they will continue collecting rents which, after all, only represent contributions by the active member in the corporation. Then one-third of this amount can be paid to the city of Montreal and another third to the province of Quebec-and if they ever decide to separate and still want to co-operate, well, they will get a third of it-and the other third, of course, will go to the federal government. Then everybody will realize that housing, neighborhood improvement and other programs will pay for themselves. But first, of course, we have to invest. If we do not invest, the situation will clearly keep on deteriorating. That is for sure, Mr. Speaker, but I will have more to say about non-profit corporations.
The government has been very active in recent years. Let's take for example the old Montreal area with its harbour and grain elevators; the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) made a statement last year about it and work is already under way. No sooner said than done. Work has already started. Montrealers will be able to get close to the port, walk through the Vieux Montreal section, and see what is going on there. The federal government has invested plenty of money in that area. Members of the opposition may have forgotten that. I hope not but in any case, I am reminding them. Now, let us go back to last april. In my riding, there is what we call Place Frontenac, a complex consisting of three high rise 15-storey buildings. My office is now located in one of them. Of course, that was in 1971. At that time, I may not have been a member of the same party but today I am on the right side and all is going fine.

Last May, the minister announced a special policy for Place Frontenac so that senior citizens could at last get housing according to their income. I was pleased with the decision at that time. Now, that is a few weeks ago, Place Frontenac became the property of the tenants of those three 15-floor high rises, that is a non-profit corporation, which should certainly enable them to pay reasonable rents with the new policy of the government. Of course, Mr. Speaker, our constituents talk about low-rental housing. Of course, to them, low rental housing means extremely low rents. Building costs being what they are today, the situation has changed considerably. Anyway, I read in La Presse this week that the minister said the shelter allowance will cost between $450 million and $1 billion a year.
It is obvious that the provincial government was supposed to go along. In fact, last year, I met the minister's assistant in Montreal. Mind you, he did not want to see me. But when I told him: If you do not, the press will know about it, I do not know if he was scared but he said: Yes, I shall meet you. I discussed with him and at some point he simply said that it was the policy of his department to establish a shelter allowance. Fine. But he added: It is not the government's policy. So you immediately see the image projected by this government which does not want to co-operate and leaves old people in ghettos, which does not want to help us help them and also leaves families in ghettos. Again last night, Mr. Speaker, when I arrived at my constituency office I had lots of people and it lasted until 11.30 p.m. There again 1 had housing problems, people coming to me for help. They go and see their alderman who says: Go and see your member of parliament, he is going to fix all that. I understand perhaps, Mr. Speaker, that Brother Andre was performing miracles but I am Brother Jack who just rings the morning bells.
Mr. Speaker, we met a few times with the Montreal mayors conference which is now in session. We talked about urban transport because that falls under urban affairs. Well, obviously, if we want to improve the economic situation in eastern Montreal-I think, of course, that I asked the question and the answer was extremely logical and I understood it as an intelligent man-we will have to follow the situation closely to determine sooner or later, as I put it to the Minister of Transport some time ago, whether it would be possible to continue the Mirabel line as far as the Angus shops. There is a big vacant lot where 8,000 housing units could be built. There is a project by Marathon, a subsidiary of Canadian Pacific, under which those units could be offered to nonprofit corporations and we could also have one of the biggest

shopping centres in Canada, and that shopping centre would operate on a co-operative basis.
Right now, according to the latest news, I am told they decided to make an industrial park out of the Angus shops and put up houses along the east-west expressway. So they are against it. I do not know if the whole world has turned topsy-turvy, but it is a fact, Mr. Speaker, that such a project with respect to the Angus plant would be very beneficial to building in the city of Montreal which is almost at a standstill. Jobs could be created in the building trades, and after the project is completed some 4,000 permanent new jobs could also be created, of which 3,000 at least do not require any special skill.
I think it is important, Mr. Speaker, to keep this in mind. Of course, this does not depend only on the federal government. I put this question before to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet). He agrees on this project. However, there is still the provincial government as well as the municipal government which controls zoning. Let us wait and see. Anyway, since we will meet with the Montreal executive council next Monday, I shall certainly raise the matter. So, I am referring to this in the House in the hope that the message will be relayed to the Quebec authorities, and as for Montreal, I will make sure to broach the subject next Monday. I usually make no bones about raising such matters.
So, Mr. Speaker, I would like to return to a point I mentioned rather briefly earlier. The rehabilitation or building of homes requires electricity, of course. Therefore I hope nobody will ever tell me some day that there is a shortage of electricity because I will start asking questions, namely whether there is still water running in the rivers. On the other hand, if we are successful, Mr. Speaker, we will have found a way of conserving energy. There is much talk about oil or other shortages. Well, if houses are electrically heated, we may then keep on using oil for other purposes as we do now and we will no longer have to worry about oil.
Mr. Speaker, people live in old houses that are not necessarily shacks. Everyone knows how much it costs to heat a home. Many families heat their homes with oil or natural gas besides electricity. Of course, this is costly! Obviously, in a constituency like the one I represent, when we consider that nearly half of the population is idle-and I hasten to add through no fault of theirs, Mr. Speaker-people have problems. In my area, we have suffered the consequences of the actions of some people, members of parliament like myself and my colleagues, who were there before us, especially in the Quebec government. We have seen nearly all the buildings on Notre-Dame Street being demolished, many businesses go bankrupt on Sainte-Catherine Street and many companies disappear. The poor guy who has lost his job and only has grade seven or eight is too old to go back to work after he has collected his unemployment insurance benefits and has to go on welfare. Imagine his problems when he finds himself in another tenement.

Mr. Speaker, I believe it is very important to be positive. Therefore I hope that if the opposition has certain amendments to suggest, they will do so now. This would be the time to do it while we are sitting in this House. We must not be content to criticize. For my part, I could criticize a lot of things if I wished, just like the opposition wants to do. I could criticize the minister and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This is why I am here. But what is important is to suggest solutions. For my part, I have some to suggest and I hope that I will have the time to submit them before my time is up.
It is quite obvious that socially and economically, the amendments to this act concerning an increase in the number of non-profit organizations will be very useful. I hope that the city of Montreal and CMHC will "thaw out" as winter is almost over and we hope that the weather will be warm enough to "thaw them out". Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few suggestions. It is rather strange, but it has always been like that in my riding. An end should come to that farce one of these days.
Mr. Speaker, when you look after your house, you tell yourself that you will make it more congenial, more comfortable. Of course, whatever happens is not to be blamed on the federal government but rather on the municipal government. They come by and raise their property taxes. I could even mention something that occurred recently in my riding where a co-operative was set up. Last summer, those who had repaired their houses, put up lovely flower boxes, had their rent increased. They are really discouraged and ready to give up.
I make this suggestion which I will repeat next Monday before the executive committee of the city of Montreal. I make it here before parliament as the federal government might participate in this project. I think that in such cases, the municipality should, when a taxpayer wants to effect improvements to his house, whether it is in Montreal or in any other municipality in this country, grant him a tax rebate to encourage him to keep his older house, and also to promote a good neighbourhood spirit.
Besides, municipalities should raise their tax rates for those who do not want to upgrade their houses for one reason: in Montreal East, the majority of shabby and dilapidated houses are owned by trusts, multimillionaires, who will have nothing to do with our working poor or senior citizens. In the meantime, their taxes are next to nothing. But the small home owner who wants to join a co-op, do something, help, get involved in the life of his community what do we do to him? We tax him. So, I feel this would first prevent speculation, and second, it would force those big corporations to do something, because we know they hate losing a buck. They would rather sell at a discount than lose money. So this could be suggested to local authorities, and the Canadian government could contribute.
To enlighten the opposition, work out the figures correctly. They are not that high. This means that if those people pay less property tax, I mean the people who improve their houses,

and if the others pay more, it will even up. The Canadian government could contribute, and even the provincial government if they wanted to. So in the end this would not be that much more expensive. It is an investment, no more, no less, and whole urban areas would be saved.
Any way this sounds quite sensible to me, and I hope the suggestion will work its way through. The opposition may also bring other suggestions.
Mr. Speaker, there is another point I would like to make: We have non-profit corporations or co-operative housing corporations. For quite some time people going to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have been given a huge pile of papers. There is a table there, the references to two months or two months and a half. A time frame is provided. You do that voluntarily, you realize that? This is voluntary. But you are given a schedule, and it takes six months before you can consider renovating a house. Think how many houses will be built at that rate! This is not in the act, it is in the regulations put out by CMHC officials. I set up another non-profit corporation in my constituency, Hochelaga. I went to the Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation and I said: We are asking for starter funds; not me personally, I only sponsor the project since, as a member of parliament I am obviously not entitled to subsidies. So I said to them: Gentlemen, we are given only $500 to start; we are given instructions, so much for this, for that and for that. I said: Gentlemen, you are way off the ball. This makes no sense whatsoever. All I ask is that you apply the National Housing Act. It is there as clear as can be.
This makes me laugh, Mr. Speaker, because all these experiences are worth relating. This makes me laugh because you submit plans which you have to be redone over and over again. And this is an expensive process. I remember the first nonprofit corporation I created in Hochelaga. A building contractor kindly offered to lend a hand. He had to redo the plans a great many times. Imagine what that would have cost us, if he had charged each time, besides the shortfall of $50,000 at 8 per cent interest per annum. It was no piece of cake, Mr. Speaker. But there is another suggestion I would like to make. I have already suggested this to CHMC. We know that non-profit corporations hire building contractors or someone to oversee the whole project, award sub-contracts, etc.; these people pocket 20 per cent of the profits. I think that we could grant by means of the National Housing Act and its regulations a certain amount of money which would go to a person who would be called the project co-ordinator and who would manage the repairs and later find a responsible person who could hire subcontractors, and it could well cost 10 per cent instead of 20 per cent. Immediately, at that very moment, costs would be reduced, because it is important, Mr. Speaker, to be cautious. You must keep in mind that even though I say those things in relation to the administration of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act and its regulations I cannot entirely blame them, because they have to be careful and I will tell you why. I think that in this House I have a right to say certain things and it is my privilege to do it. I will

not mention any names. I will simply say that some people belonging to the organization of the Progressive Conservative party, who were part of my own organization at that time, did try to entice me into a gimmick involving $10,000 in pay-offs in connection with non-profit housing, and that I never accepted such offers. But it would seem that somebody got these $10,000. I even asked the RCMP to investigate but nothing could be done in that case. So I certainly hope that public interest will still be protected, but there should also be more flexibility and it should be possible, Mr. Speaker, to get housing to move faster because it is much too slow now. It is a never ending process.
What is happening now is that people working on a voluntary basis are discouraged by these procedures and stop working. The law is there to provide for everything needed, but appropriate formulas have to be found in co-operation with the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to make housing procedures easier and faster. There is also an important point, probably one of the last, Mr. Speaker, about which I am very happy. It is obvious that the bill before the House is aimed at increasing the participation of the private sector, that is credit unions and banks, by allowing mortgages on non-profit housing.
Of course, through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation the federal government will guarantee these loans up to 100 per cent. I intended to put a question to the minister, and I suppose that he expected it. I hope that with these guarantees the private sector will co-operate and will not have the nerve to turn down non-profit corporations. Certainly, it could say no to a corporation which is not serious, because the authorization of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation would still be needed. There are obviously many people working for the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It is not necessarily because of that that the process takes so much time. It is because when you go there with a document, it has to go through the hands of about eight people. They must obviously have enough time to examine it. But it seems to me it is possible to speed things up.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I urge the parties of the opposition to support this bill. Naturally, the government is open to any amendment to the bill; that is why we are here, to find solutions to problems. But, above all else I hope we will think of the old, of those among us who are less fortunate, who are in need of housing.
If, at some point, we could considerably increase the number of non-profitable corporations, if every hon. member in this House could set up that type of committee, in his riding, specifically to increase the number of housing corporations or co-operatives, I feel we could help one another speed up the construction of houses. Indeed, when you live in a house where you are cold, where you have to pay twice as much as others for heating, especially this year when winter has been rather severe, life is not easy for people.
I trust that the first goal of hon. members in this House is, first and foremost, to put the interest of all Canadians ahead

of party or personal interests. That is the wish I express for the benefit of all hon. members trusting they will do the same.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to intervene in this debate on Bill C-29. I might say that when I read the bill I was not surprised at the contents. Everyone who has been on the receiving end of the government's policies over the past seven or eight years is well aware of the difficulty the government has had, first, in shaping its policies and, second, in implementing them.
Essentially, the bill does three things. First, it disentangles the mess which the government has created in housing at both provincial and municipal levels over the last seven years; second, it cuts out the government's financial commitment to housing and urban affairs and, third, it winds down the Ministry of Urban Affairs after its death was announced in 1978. That is really what the bill does on behalf of the government. It disentangles, it cuts losses, and it winds down the ministry. That is what most people thought would be the case.
I was surprised, though, to hear the minister speaking in defence of the bill. Despite what the legislation was saying, he seemed to approach the subject with no sense of humility about what has happened in the last seven years. I read his speech again to make sure that I had fully understood it. This was not a minister trying to explain why things had gone wrong. It was not a speech in which he sought to indicate there were other ways in which things could be done. Here was a minister trying to shine up the unshineable and to polish up the unpolishable. It was unbelievable.
In attempting to draw a rosy picture of unsullied success in the last seven years, in order to put some flesh on these bones, what did the minister do? He took credit for making sure we had hot and cold running water. That is to be found in black and white on page 3544 of Hansard. As recorded on the same page, the minister took credit for stabilizing the price of housing. It is true he only picks out one year-1977-and it is correct to say that prices went up only 3 per cent in that year. But would he dare tell us by how much the price had gone up since 1968 when this government took over, or since 1970 when this ministry was established?
Every Canadian knows that the price of housing has doubled in ten years, and more than doubled in some areas. It is appalling that the minister should try to polish up the handle of the big brass door by saying it went up 3 per cent in 1977.
I think it is important that what this legislation says is put into perspective. What does it say to the people of this country? First let us talk about the things it says to people who live in substandard housing. That is a concern of the minister. He said he was worried about that. In 1973 a good philosophy was introduced. A good program, the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, was introduced. I recall being here in a committee of this House in 1973 and urging the policy on the then minister. It was a good concept and a good philoso-
