phy. Basically what it said was that increasingly in the older areas in the cities of this country-

-and towns and villages as well, including Burks Falls, there was housing stock which needed to be rehabilitated. At the outset there were certain restrictions placed on RRAP. First, it was available only to people who earned less than $ 11,000. Second, it was available only in certain designated areas in those cities, towns and villages, primarily areas which were known later as neighbourhood improvement areas for non-profit and co-op housing projects, and therefore usually older areas.
Those two restrictions were very important. The first one, the $11,000 income cut-off level was cut out, I think, in 1975. I am not sure of the year, but it was a couple of years ago. However, the money was still confined to designated neighbourhood improvement areas. There was one small difficulty with that designation, and that is that there were some areas, some streets and some housing just outside those NIP areas which also should have received some of the money. So there needed to be written into the legislation some small amount of flexibility. What the minister did about that small need was unbelievable. On December 12 of 1978 he announced that from then on in, the rehabilitation program would not be confined to NIP areas. RRAP was going to be universal. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) will remember that. A universal program for RRAP was announced on December 12, 1978.
The minister was cautioned by CMHC officials. Hon. members may recall the letter written on January 3 by a very worried president of CMHC, Mr. Hession, to the minister. The first paragraph says, and I quote:
I am writing in regard to the availability of funds under the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program. Since the announcement of December 12, 1978 about the proposed removal of statutory area constraints on the program, we have been receiving calls from the media and members of the public at large on this subject, and it is important that we know how best to respond.
You bet! Poor old CMHC had to take all the calls from people across Canada saying they would like to have their RRAP money because the minister said it was universal. Poor old CMHC had to say it did not have the amount of money required. In fact on January 3 the president of CMHC pointed out to the minister, and I quote:
The 1979 capital budget is $56 million. We will need $37 million to maintain activity in the existing designated areas where work has already begun. A further $3 million will be needed to deal with areas already designated but where work has not started. This leaves $16 million of the 1979 budget for new initiatives. However, 68 areas have already submitted final applications for designation under the 1978 rules. After the new law comes into effect, they will not need order in council designation, but they will warrant some priority attention ... Thus, only $9 million for some 2,250 units remains for work under the terms of the new program criteria once the bill is passed.
The president of CMHC also told the minister the following:
This is a fairly modest amount and we should avoid raising expectations which we cannot satisfy.
Housing
What does the president of CMHC propose once this bill is passed?
I would like simply to note that it would appear virtually impossible to establish a system which does not involve the selection of areas for priority action, even though accommodation can be made for scattered site applications too.
Well, son of a gun! We are right back to designated areas again. In fact, so concerned is Mr. Hession-not was, but is- that he was pleased to offer the minister a backgrounder so that the minister would at least get some grasp of what he was saying. He sent the minister a backgrounder, a ten-year plan to modernize and rehabilitate Canada's housing stock. He wanted the minister at least to look at it. I will not go through the four pages. I will just read the last part. It says, and I quote:
What it means in the briefest terms is that while a considerable number of people can take action in the near future, because their areas and homes are in bad shape, others will need to wait for a while. It also means that the rehabilitation effort will continue to be concentrated in specified action areas as in the past-
That could not be any plainer. There is a reason why CMHC has to do that. It does not have the money to have a universal program. That did not stop the minister, by the way. He said in December that it is a universal program. The president of CMHC wrote him a letter and said, in effect, "Please don't do that, sir; we don't have the money, and you are just going to raise expectations and disappoint people." Yesterday when the minister spoke in the House he did not use the word "universal". He went further, if one can go further than universal. He said that it is a program, and I quote, "available to all of Canada." He said that in the face of the letter he received from the president of CMHC.
The reason I dwell on that is because in so much of the housing and urban affairs policy of this government since 1970 it has not been policy which has dominated. It has been public relations which have dominated and motivated pronouncements, announcements, and ultimately retractions, because of the way this government has proceeded with respect to urban Canada. That has hurt people. Many people say that a certain program is good and that because the minister says they can get money they would like to fix up their houses. The fact is that there is no money. Public relations are not policy. People who are interested in rehabilitating their homes do not trust the policy of this government.
What does this legislation say to the neighbourhoods and communities of this country which want to improve themselves? I speak now of the so-called community services grants program. The community services grants program is really a merging of three previous programs. The first is the Neighbourhood Improvement Program which expired last March. It was a very good program since its inception in 1973. In fact, since 1975, $200 million has been involved. I give fair marks to the government on a very good program. That was the first program. The second program is the Municipal Incentives Grants Program which was to offer incentives with respect to the medium-density, low-cost housing in municipalities in this country. That expired last December. The third is the Municipal Infrastructure Program. Although the minister took credit

March 1, 1979
Housing
for it, it began in 1961. If I recall history-and of course the Minister of Agriculture can correct me-I think we had a Conservative government at that time. Since 1961 $1.5 billion has been coming from that program in the last 17 years to the municipalities of this country.
The minister could have taken credit for these three things. Those are things that have really happened and that have helped people and helped neighbourhoods. In fact, there was some thought about taking the three programs and merging them into a community services grant program, block funding, and using those funds as well for rinks, community halls and community centres. In fact, block funding was recommended to the ministry in the standing committee in 1973. I know because I made the recommendation myself. So I am glad to see the principle of block funding finally there six years later. But again, what is the way to deal with the problem? Offer the policy, implement it, and try to be known by your good works alone? Not this government. Here is the press release of May, 1978, put out by the minister on this matter. The bill was only brought here in March of 1979, but in May of 1978 the press release from the minister stated the following:
Quietly, without a lot of fanfare, the hon. Andre Ouellet has moved with his provincial counterparts to decisively alter the relationships between the federal and provincial governments in the housing and community services fields.
By the way, that is not new, that came out in the press release last May. What happened since last May? Knock on the door of any municipality in this country right now, or telephone them, and they will tell you that in the last 18 months or almost two years there has been nothing but delay, anxiety, and confusion in the municipalities as to what the heck this government intends to do and when they will do it. They do not know what assistance is available under the community services program. They do not know what assistance has been withdrawn and they do not know anything about the implementation dates of any assistance that might still be there. If you do not believe that, call the municipalities in your own riding, because essentially what the government did do was to paralyse the ability of the municipalities to plan both in terms of land use and in terms of their capital budgets, because you cannot plan if you do not know how much money you will get for sewage, for medium density low cost housing, or for NIP. So every municipality in this country which has those programs available to them has been unable to implement them for what amounts to two fiscal years.
Interestingly enough, as most people know, capital budget time for municipalities come just about now. Most municipalities have already prepared their budgets, so it will not help them this year. What the government has given the municipalities is delay and confusion with regard to the community services program. In fact, when you read the fine print, you find that at least the old Neighbourhood Improvement Program gave 25 per cent in front end money, that is to say, you have 25 cents on the dollar early on so you can use the money to plan with it. That is cut out now. We are back to the old urban renewal idea of the municipality doing it, charging it,

and then recovering the money. That is not great, but it is okay for a city like Montreal or Toronto, it may be all right for Winnipeg or Calgary, but it is not very good for medium-sized or small-sized municipalities. They cannot put the money in the budget. That is why NIP provided them with an opportunity to do their planning early. Read this bill and you will find that such a provision is not contained in it. That is why you will not need much money for the NIP portion of the municipality services program because people have not been able to plan for it.
What does this mean? The government brought this program to a standstill. The municipalities are not using it. Do you know what that means, particularly when you deal with NIP in any neighbourhood? You have to put together an organization of people and you have to keep them going and interested in their work. The only way they keep on being interested is when they have the bucks to do the job. Nobody likes to continue talking forever and have nothing done. If you get to a situation, as is the case in Toronto, in Montreal, and in all major cities as well as in medium-sized cities-there is a mayor or two across the way who knows from previous times the point I am making-where you want to keep up interest in neighbourhood improvement, you must make sure the money is flowing. I am telling you, it is not flowing now. Telephone any municipality in your own riding. The hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) can phone City Hall in Toronto and find that out right now. In fact she can phone Paul Ringer and find out.
Call the province of Ontario.

Third, what is this legislation saying to the people who pay more than they should out of the income they have for the housing they get? These people pay more than is reasonable, according to home economists, more than they should be paying for housing, given the size of their income. We are advised that there are 438,000 people in this country who pay more than 30 per cent of their income, and there are 800,000-it does not seem like much if you say it fast but it is a lot if you say it slowly-800,000 households paying more than 25 per cent. What do you say about that? What does the bill say about it, and what does the minister say about it? At page 3546 of Hansard of February 23 the minister is reported to have said the following:
But in their case, and I say it again, theirs is not so much a problem of housing as one of income.
How do you like that? I know the Minister of Agriculture would agree that if prices of food went up 300 per cent, he could use the same argument, that the problem is not one of food but one of income. If there were a 1,000 per cent increase in the cost of furniture, it would not be a furniture problem but an income problem.
The minister went on to say the following, and this is the best part:
For them, as hon. members know, I announced earlier this week, in a speech I made in Toronto, that there was another solution to their problem,
March 1, 1979

So he announced a solution. He is the minister responsible, he is not a backbencher like myself, he is not like the Minister of Agriculture, so as the minister responsible in this area, can he go and say, "Well, this seems like a reasonable idea to me. I will do a little wool gathering, I do not have to promise anything, I do not have to do anything about it. What I can do is try to stop people from worrying"? What was so galling about that was that he announced this solution as though he was struck on the road to Damascus, as though he had never heard about it before, as though he uncovered something new for people. In 1972 the department received a series of recommendations in a wonderful book called "Programs in Search of a Policy". It is a title at which the government should look. It is a book on low income housing in Canada written by Michael Dennis and Susan Fish. At page 354 of that report there is a section called "Shelter Allowances". That is what the minister was talking about the other day. I cannot read the entire section because it is approximately ten pages in length.
The first sentence indicates the difficulties of making a building subsidy program work. This leads the authors to recommend a shelter allowance program as the only workable alternative. Also it is indicated that there are many variations in the form such assistance could take. It could be a rent certificate, a rent rebate, a generalized allowance. It could be made payable in the case of tenancy or ownership. It could be payable to an individual or his landlord. It might be payable only to families with children, the elderly, the disabled, or it could be paid to all households. It might depend upon living in adequate housing. It might vary with income, size of family or size of community. These are some of the variations to which the co-authors referred. Then it goes on to offer comments on the experience in Germany, Holland, Sweden, Denmark, Italy and a few other countries.
Shelter allowances which the minister talked about in Toronto are not new. In fact shelter allowances were recommended to the government six years ago. For the minister to suggest that it is somehow an alternative which he thought up for the election, is something for which he will have to answer. By the way, if I had not read from that publication, I could have offered another one. The Canadian Council on Social Development came out with a report on the matter a couple of months ago. They made the same argument as Michael Dennis and Susan Fish six years ago. It has been around a long time, and I might add that it is a good policy. The idea of a home shelter allowance is a good one. It has certain advantages. Essentially it would assist people rather than buildings. That is the basic philosophical difference between it and home subsidy. It would assist people rather than buildings.
Housing
What are the advantages?

The advantages are many. It would cut out waiting lists. There would be no more waiting lists, no more interviews, no more walking around and waiting for someone else to decide where one can live. It would offer an increase in choice. One could live in a number of places. It diminishes the consequences. It broadens the choice. It diminishes socio-economic ghettos. Also it diminishes the stigma of assisted housing which unfortunately still exists. It is more cheaply done. There are studies to show that. If the costs are added up, all the ones which can be seen and all the ones which cannot be seen in terms of subsidizing buildings, it will be found that subsidizing people is cheaper. I might add that it reaches more people in need.
There are difficulties as well. It is with considerable regret that I indicate the government did not spend time studying all alternatives available respecting shelter allowances in the last six years. Approximately six years after the government received the recommendation, airily the minister said that it is a germ of a good idea. We could have been on to a program of home shelter allowances previously. There are a number which have been established partially in the country. I think the minister should have started some years ago by saying, "Let us begin with senior citizens".
There is a program in British Columbia which other hon. members have mentioned already, Safer. Not only is there a program in place, but the government had studies available to tell it how well the program was doing. It is a very good program. The minister could have studied that program. In fact the minister could have monitored that program over the last three years, and he could have brought in one by 1979. The program could have dealt with senior citizens as well as people below the poverty line. We have shown that subsidizing buildings for people below the poverty line is not the way to go. The way to go is with home shelter allowances. The speech of the minister in Toronto typified the manner in which municipal affairs, urban affairs and housing generally are treated by the government.
The government is interested in public relations. It has no policies. What does it say to tenants in the country? Nothing. The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) has mentioned that already. One can go through the bill. What does it say to tenants anywhere in the country? Absolutely nothing. There is no shelter allowance program. The minister had six years to bring in such a program. There is no shelter allowance program for tenants. There is no longer an assisted rental program. Most hon. members are not aware of the fact that there is no ARP any more. The vacancy rate in the city of Toronto is .9 per cent. In the rest of Ontario it is somewhere between 1.5 per cent and 2 per cent. Major cities are closer to the Toronto percentage of .9. I am not aware of the figures in other parts of the country. I can dwell only on Ontario figures. The only way to relieve the low vacancy rate, and therefore be able to contribute something toward reducing the price of
3746

March 1, 1979
Housing
rental housing, is to produce more. Thus, tenants would have cheaper rents. There is no allowance. There is no ARP. There is nothing for tenants in this bill.
What does it say to home owners? It says nothing to tenants, and what it says to home owners is worse than nothing. The single most important thing which happened to home owners as a consequence of this bill is that the Assisted Home Ownership Program has been knocked out and the Graduated Mortgage Payment Program put in. AHOP out, GMP in. I think some hon. members have dealt already with the Graduated Mortgage Payment program. I should like to put one or two thoughts forward. One economist said the following:
Administered by the CMHC, GMP's are designed to give a house buyer one of the major advantages already provided by AHOP: during the first five years of a graduated payment mortgage, monthly payments are much lower than a conventional mortgage would allow. From then on, payments are stepped up gradually until after the tenth year, when they reach a plateau.
Of course this allows the person to get in earlier with a low downpayment.
The economist continued with the part the government does not want to mention. He said the following:
But the unpleasant, less obvious fact is that over the life of the debt, the GMP will cost the borrower $9,324 more than the standard mortgage would- $105,024, compared with $95,700.
He borrows $35,000 and he will pay back $105,024. Bad farming, bad farming.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That comment is for you, Eugene.

In fact it is so bad that Peter Carter, the past chairman of the mortgage committee on Canadian banking calls it "permadebt". That is pretty chilly. It is like stagflation. Permadebt applies to the individual; stagflation apparently applies to society. It is no more or less than an economic bondage, that is what it means. It is economic bondage. Hon. members should think of themselves being involved in it. It is all right to talk about other people, but how would hon. members like to be in it? There was a time up until approximately seven or eight years ago when people regarded buying a home, particularly first time buyers, as a way of getting ahead in the country. With permadebt, the government's mortgage answer, it is becoming a way to get behind. That is what has been done to housing. It is not how people see it in terms of getting ahead, it is how one puts oneself behind. Not only that, but the banks will have difficulty because it does not make any economic sense. The government comes along and says what it is going to do is pay off all the debts after 90 days. Nobody likes to be in debt. Even the banks do not like to be in debt.
What this bill means to home owners is that they will be in bondage. Secondly, it perverts the principles of good banking in order to cover this government's act. Thirdly, and perhaps I should mention this as I have not heard anyone else refer to it, the graduated payment mortgage plan also has built into it,

depending on taxes and fuel, a five per cent to seven per cent inflation factor. How is that for wrestling inflation to the ground? The government is building inflation into its own mortgage plan. This is what it does for home owners.
What does it do for the construction industry? There is no AHOP program left so the industry can not use it. There is no assisted home ownership plan left at all, and there is no assisted rental program, so you cannot take advantage of that. This means, of course, there will be no multi-dwelling projects constructed.
There is the suggestion that somehow the market is already supplying enough. As someone has pointed out, we have the wrong kind of housing in the wrong places and we do not have the right kind of houses in the right places. What this essentially means to the construction industry, and let that industry here this loud and clear, is that there will be no construction and no jobs. The unemployment level in the construction industry, certainly in Ontario, is at a record high since the depression. What this bill says to the construction industry is that there will be no development, no construction, and no jobs.
When listening to members speak, particularly those of the other two parties, I heard them repeatedly say they are universally against the mortgage interest and property tax deductibility policy. I took that phrase from the minister, but these people have spoken in condemnation of that program. Indeed, one day the minister had a little fun with me when he referred to my statement that it required some further thought. Indeed, I did say it required some further thought. It requires some further thought, in my view, in relation to the shelter allowance. It seemed to me, and still does, that a shelter allowance, particularly for senior citizens and those living below the poverty line, is a policy worthy of any government.
When one member after another stood and talked about the mortgage interest and property tax deductibility program as a bad thing, I concluded they had not read it and did not care to read it. At least this program offers something to the home owners and to the people who want to own homes and want their children to own homes. Indeed, knock on the doors of senior citizens and I suggest they will tell you they would like to see their grandchildren own homes. If you ask them, I expect the answer you would get is yes. At least this policy offers something to home owners and those who would like to be home owners. It will not put them into economic bondage. What it does is offer the hope of home ownership in this country. The program does offer something to those who pay too much of their income for housing. This bill does absolutely nothing in this regard, and the government has said nothing about this, with the exception of that fly-by-night speech of the minister last week.
What our program suggests is that it will be cheaper to own a home, that it will reduce the amount of income the people have to pay to own homes, and that this will make home ownership more affordable. There is absolutely nothing in this
March 1, 1979

bill in that regard. Not only does it offer nothing to home owners, it offers nothing to everyone who pays more of their income than they should for housing.
I would like my colleagues in the NDP to think of this. Our proposal will benefit the construction industry. After removing the anxiety in respect of the oversupply in the market in those areas where units have been built in the wrong places, our policy will stimulate construction, which in turn will create more jobs in that industry, and in other areas such as furniture manufacturing, appliance manufacturing, textiles, the needle trades and so on. These sectors need the jobs which will only follow stimulation in construction activity.
What does this bill do in respect of co-operatives and the non-profit organizations? I have been very impressed by the new love affair people are having in respect of service clubs, labour councils, cultural groups and religious institutions now engaged in non-profit housing. I have been involved for 12 or 13 years with non-profit housing and co-ops, indeed at a time when people did not talk about them in polite society. I do not think I have to offer my credentials, or point out the significance of non-profit corporations and co-ops in large cities and neighbourhoods.
The minister says this is the best part of the bill, and the non-profit organizations and co-ops want this legislation. They really do want it. Their tongues are hanging out for it because they have been held up in some cases for almost two years waiting for the minister to bring this into the house. That is why they want it.

Mr. Speaker, my intervention in this debate will be quite limited. I have been concerned, as have other members of my party and of the government, about the insistence by hon. members in the opposition, and I do not refer to the NDP, on the value of the mortgage interest and real estate deductibility program in having a stimulative effect on the housing industry, and in achieving the great American dream, as the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott) is often wont to call it, of owning your own home. I do not suggest that because 1 think their hearts are not in the right place, but because I believe that, on serious examination of the type we have conducted on this side of the House, they will see the program is not one that will achieve those objectives.
Housing
It is reasonable to presume that we in Canada would not even be considering such a plan or program were it not to exist in the United States and not to have been popularized, if you like, by our American neighbour to the south. Because of that I welcomed the opportunity to visit Washington several weeks ago in a bipartisan parliamentary group consisting of, from our side of the House, the hon. member for Stormont-Dundas (Mr. Lumley); from the other side of the House the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke), and the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Rae). We had the opportunity of examining in depth with a very wide cross-section of American officials who are responsible for the administration of this particular law and, of course, all other fiscal laws. For example there was the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, the policy division of the Department of the Treasury, the Congressional Budget Committee, the Joint Committee on Taxation, as well as independent economists from the Brookings Institution, the American Enterprise Institute, and various other experts in the field.
This was done in the spirit of objective examination to determine whether or not the deductibility of mortgage interest and real estate taxes is a valuable device in achieving the objectives that have been put forward by the opposition for examination, namely, home ownership, stimulation of the economy, and perhaps some fiscal relief to create more tax neutrality in the income tax system.
I think that I can say, without fear of contradiction, that the opinion of all informed observers in the United States is to the effect that mortgage interest deductibility and real estate tax deductibility does not accomplish any of those objectives and that those objectives can be better achieved by other techniques. Going further than that, I believe it is important for us in Canada to understand why interest in the United States is deductible in computing income and why real estate taxes are deductible. I would like very briefly to provide this House with some of the background of the American experience.
Beginning with the Internal Revenue Code of 1913 it was recognized that interest in general, not just interest on mortgages, all interest, should be deductible, as well as local taxes. Hence it was built into the very structure of the American income tax system from the outset. That, to begin with, is to be contrasted dramatically with the situation in Canada where local taxes are not deductible. So, it is apparent to even the most unsophisticated observer that rendering real estate taxes deductible, for example, would automatically at the local level create a shift of local taxation into real estate taxes.
It seems to me that nothing could be more obvious, and it was pointed out to us by our American observers that such would inevitably be the case.
But over the years, because of these deductions, our U.S. neighbours have designed standard deductions across the board applicable to U.S. taxpayers. I believe that at the

March 1, 1979
Housing
present time in 1978 or 1979-I may be speaking in 1978 figures, I am not certain-a single taxpayer in the United States is entitled to a basic $2,300 deduction, and a married couple is entitled to a $3,400 deduction. That deduction absorbs this wide variety of local taxes and interest which they would otherwise have to itemize and, hence, 75 per cent of U.S. taxpayers who file returns in the United States file them on the basis of unitemized returns taking that basic deduction. On the other hand, 25 per cent of the returns that are filed are filed on the so-called long itemized return.
We were advised by the internal revenue authorities that in such cases the returns are necessary because of these specific deductions, that the deductions for mortgage interest and real estate taxes push people into such high deductions that it is worth their while to claim these deductions on the long form. In fact were it not for these specific deductions the entire U.S. tax system could be considerably simplified. I might add that the cost to the U.S. treasury in 1978 for this specific deduction was estimated to be $12.8 billion.
Before dealing with some of the specific problems which are inherent in the scheme, I think it is very important to underline the fact that in the United States 63 per cent of housing is owner occupied and 37 per cent is rented. The figures, of course, vary from area to area. For example, in New York state the rental percentage is higher and the ownership percentage is lower. It struck all of us in the group, interestingly enough, that those figures corresponded indentically with the numbers that have been furnished to us by Statistics Canada 1976, namely, 63 per cent of the housing in this country is owner occupied and 37 per cent is rented. Again there are variations from region to region, and in my particular province the percentages are almost 50-50. As a matter of fact, I believe the figures are 49 and 51.
It is interesting to note that notwithstanding the existence of this so-called benefit of mortgage interest deductibility over all these years, owner occupied housing in this country has kept pace with that in the United States, and we were further advised, although I have not verified these numbers, but I intend to do so, that upon their analysis in the United States the lower income groups in Canada had a higher percentage of home ownership than in their country, and the reverse was true, of course, in higher income groups. All of this speaks well for the experience that Canadians have had in housing people in this country and in providing that great American dream which the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton refers to, namely, home ownership.
I for one subscribe to the value of home ownership and I think that most of us do. It is not something which can be defined. Again, in the course of discussions with economists and others who had conducted an analysis in this area, it was felt that there was no demonstrable evidence that home ownership per se had inherent value. Nevertheless, my own feeling is that home ownership is a good thing. I think that a stake in our country and our communities, an asset of that kind, is bound to create and encourage stability and responsibility.

Let us assume that members on all sides of this House are in agreement that home ownership is a desirable objective. As I have said, I certainly endorse that principle, as do, I am sure, all members of my party. But how can it best be achieved? That is the question to which we must address ourselves. I have noticed that in most of the comments made by the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton in the press she has stated on many occasions, and I think sincerely and basically with the best of good will, that home ownership is desirable and that this plan is designed to achieve home ownership. Let us look at the plan for a moment and let us determine whether it really does accomplish its purpose.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR REGULAR JET SERVICE INTO WESTERN MANITOBA
AIR TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR REGULAR JET SERVICE INTO WESTERN MANITOBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday 16 I pursued yet another time the question of jet air service into western Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan. I directed my question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). He was kind enough to indicate that he realizes that improved air service is needed. This was on the basis of the warm reception he received when he was in Brandon for the opening of the Winter Games some two weeks ago. He said, finally, that he did not understand why the people of Brandon should want to leave such a fine centre quickly. Unfortunately, I was not able to ask a supplementary. Had I had that privilege I would have responded that it was not a case of leaving the city of Brandon or the area of western Manitoba, but rather, as the old adage says, all wise men come from the east, and the wiser they are the faster they come! It is because there is a great demand to get into this part of the country that we need the jet service for ingress and egress.
The problem simply is that we have in place at the moment-and I suppose it was put in place so that the government would be able to say there was air service available for the Winter Games-and, incidentally, as everyone knows, the community of Brandon, which is the smallest ever to have staged the games, did the best job that has ever been done in this respect-we have in place a commuter air service provided by Perimeter Aviation Ltd. This does not operate from the main air terminal in Winnipeg. Passengers are bussed to the back of the airport where they climb on board a small aircraft. It is almost necessary to get into the aircraft on hands
March 1, 1979

and knees. On the occasions that I have tried it, senior citizens have not been able to get in, and it would be absolutely impossible for handicapped people to use the aircraft.
This service will only be successful, as was demonstrated when we had a commuter service before, if it is linked into the direct air service in the excellent, brand new terminal facilities at the western Manitoba airport directly south of the city of Brandon. We cannot make it economically viable if we are merely a satellite of the international air terminal that services the city of Winnipeg.
The irony of the situation is that all major airlines fly over this lovely new terminal facility. Pacific Western, Air Canada and CPA have regular flights daily over the airport. If we had a sky hook that would hook on at 30,000 feet, we could use the facilities.
I have examined the timetables of these airlines, Mr. Speaker. Air Canada flies out of Ottawa, Toronto, London and into Winnipeg, directly over the city of Brandon. I have taken the flight on many occasions to see how great is the passenger load. Passengers are not available for that flight in any greater numbers than would be provided by the 200,000 citizens who live in the western Manitoba area.
I flew Pacific Western out of Yellowknife recently. It picked up passengers at Yellowknife in a 737, to go to High River, Pine Point and on to Edmonton. Those communities are much smaller than the 200,000 population that is available for jet service in the western Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan area.
I am interested in the CPA schedule. It at least recognizes that there is a city of Brandon because it links it with Winnipeg. Neither PWA nor Air Canada acknowledges that there is even such a community as Brandon. During the Winter Games it was necessary to bring in some 3,000 amateur athletes from all parts of Canada by charter aircraft. It was amazing to see the efficiency with which those airlines of all types flew into Brandon and were handled by the fully equipped airport. The manpower is there and the terminals facilities are there. All we need is the aircraft.
It was certainly demonstrated during the Winter Games that this airport is fully equipped to provide the best level of service that is available. It should also handle charter flights. The Sunflight business in the winter is a tremendously profitable activity. This service could easily be handled with our large parking area.
The international terminal at Winnipeg requires expansion. No longer can the parking facilities there meet the demand of the large number of passengers using that airport. The Government of Canada has invested in the terminal. It is there. All we ask is a service similar to that offered to the community of Dryden. I have looked at the new Nordair schedule of service. They fly in and out of Dryden at least twice a day, even though it is a much smaller community and has a much smaller population than the 200,000 in the western Manitoba area.
Adjournment Debate
I discussed this matter with the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, now the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Reid), who represents a community in a position similar to the western Manitoba area. He is sympathetic.
Now that it has been demonstrated that there is a real need and that the facilities are available, I hope that at long last the government will discharge the promise it made during the 1974 election and that western Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan, including Yorkton which has no air service, will be provided with service on the scale promised in 1974.

speakeroldname: Mr. Raymond Dupont (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR REGULAR JET SERVICE INTO WESTERN MANITOBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), suggests that during the electoral campaign of 1974, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) promised a regular jet service to western Manitoba. I think he is referring to the speech the Prime Minister made in Winnipeg on May 23, 1974. I would like to quote part of that speech to show that the government has kept its electoral promises. The Prime Minister said:
Now, I would like to talk about another sector of the air service, about the air policy, about industrial development and job creation. Indeed, I would like to announce that the government has approved in principle the establishment of an air service between Winnipeg, Brandon, Dauphin, Yorkton and Saskatoon in order to try out new policies for third level air services. Air services will be established between these centres of Western Canada.
The Prime Minister certainly did not suggest a jet service, but rather a local carrier or third level carrier type of service which never uses jet aircraft. Although nobody on the electoral campaign trail promised a jet service for Brandon, my hon. colleague knows full well that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has done his utmost to try and get such a service for that community. In 1977 the minister announced that the government was prepared to grant financial assistance up to $1.1 million for the operation of a jet service between Brandon, Toronto and Regina. He asked interested carriers to file an application with the Canadian Transport Commission. Unfortunately, his offer did not meet with the expected response.
Despite the position taken by carriers on this matter in 1977, once again late last fall the minister tried to obtain a jet service for Brandon. As the minister himself explained, he has had repeated disucssions with airline representatives to encourage them to file an application for an east-west jet service. He also stated that he was ready to give all necessary assistance to ensure that such application would be granted. Yet no carrier took heed. At present, Brandon has an excellent air service, operated twice a day by Perimeter Airlines, which receives financial assistance from the government.

NATIONAL DEFENCE-SUGGESTION OVERSEAS ARMED FORCES PERSONNEL RECEIVE FREE MAILING PRIVILEGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, February 21, I put a question to the Minister of National

March 1, 1979
Adjournment Debate
Defence (Mr. Danson) having to do with the free mailing privilege which some of our armed forces personnel engaged in United Nations peacekeeping operations receive. I was making inquiries into the possibility of this privilege being extended to all Canadian servicemen overseas.
The minister told the House he was not aware that any of our armed forces personnel were receiving those privileges. I did not have an opportunity to get back to him with a supplementary question assuring him that my information was correct, but the minister rose on a point of order on February 23 to clarify the matter, stating that though, as he had indicated, the Canadian government and the Department of National Defence do not accord free mail privileges to service personnel, the United Nations Emergency Force in the Middle East does benefit from free mailing privileges provided by the United Nations.
Recently, I was in the Middle East along with five other members of this chamber. We had the privilege of touring the various posts at which Canadian forces are stationed and we found this question of mail facilities was a bone of contention among those to whom free mailing privileges had not been extended. I raised this matter so that the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) could give consideration to extending free mailing privileges to all members of our armed forces who do such a commendable job as a peacekeeping force. When these men are absent abroad for tours of six months, communication with their homes is essential if they are to keep in touch with their families. In view of the fact that the dollar has fallen considerably in value, and since responsibility for this decline must fall squarely on the shoulders of members opposite, it seems fair something should be done to minimize its effect upon them. Our armed forces are doing a superb job in the Middle East and I would ask ministers seriously to consider offering free mailing privileges to our armed forces personnel posted overseas.

speakeroldname: Mr. Raymond Dupont (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-SUGGESTION OVERSEAS ARMED FORCES PERSONNEL RECEIVE FREE MAILING PRIVILEGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must point out that the men and women of the Canadian armed forces now offer their expertise and leadership abroad. In this unique field of international responsibility, and this is a well known fact, Canada continues to receive praise and encouragement, and I have come to understand why through my work as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson). This is reflected in the pride of each member of the Canadian armed forces.
Those among us who have had the opportunity to see them in action can understand the pride felt by Canadians when they travel in Europe and can note for themselves the excellent reputation that Canada has gained through the peacetime efforts of our armed forces. This is something we cannot and would not want to forget. Mr. Speaker, I would also like to make a comment concerning the thousands of men and women in the Canadian armed forces, many of them with their

families, who serve Canada abroad. Many of these Canadians are members of our NATO forces and they are treated in the same way as any other Canadian citizen abroad.
We are aware of the fact that inflation affects Canadians serving in Europe and that our service people are no exception to this rule. I must however note with great satisfaction that our military personnel is very well paid, at a level equivalent to the employees of the public service of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I want to reassure the hon. member that the interest he has shown as well as other very important things- that we consider continuing in our efforts to ensure that our servicemen in this country will keep on getting the benefits they deserve in addition to what they earn. My colleague mentioned in this House on February 23 last, when he raised a question of privilege that UN Forces in the Middle East get free mailing privileges for their members for up to five letters a week not exceeding one ounce per letter, under a special arrangement. Such letters are mailed free under arrangements entered upon by the UN Emergency Forces and postage is paid by them.
Mr. Speaker, I want to say to my colleague that according to the minister each force had its own procedural rules. However, he will follow up on this thing and find out whether other UN forces could be allowed the same privileges. I can assure the hon. member that this is going through the appropriate channels to see what might be done to arrange that. As the hon. member probably knows, our Canadian servicemen have served with distinction and pride as UN members engaged in peace-keeping operations ever since our former Prime Minister, the Right Hon. EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-GOVERNMENT'S INSTRUCTIONS TO CANADIAN DELEGATION AT BELGRADE CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) to answer a very simple question. I wanted the minister to tell parliament and the people of Canada if it was true that our Canadian delegation in Belgrade, reviewing the Helsinki Accords, was instructed not to protest the violations of the accords by specifically naming the violating states and the victims of their violations. The minister could easily have answered yes or no. He could easily have explained. The minister has acquired a reputation for his agility and ability as an excellent speaker in the House. He is quite capable of manoeuvring his way out of the toughest questions. Yet there was no answer. There was only silence, the silence of excuses,
March 1, 1979

of insecurity and doubt, the same silence that dominated the negotiations at Belgrade. It was the silence of hesitancy and fear to stand up boldly and speak out. It was the eternal silence of cocktail diplomacy, fearing to stand firm on one's principles and convictions with the courage to speak the truth from the heart and from the soul because it may insult the violator. Violators are not insulted, and we must confront them with truth, for it is they who insult the humanity and the honesty of men of good will who trusted and believed that agreements would be respected.
So, equally, our silence is an insult to Canada, whose people do not want to be partners in lies and deceit. Canada has contributed in a major way to the struggle for human rights. It was this country which provided leadership in formulating and including the humanitarian clauses of the Helsinki Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe in 1975.
Our country, and its government, more than any other of the western democratic states which signed the accords, have moral responsibility for the fate of those human beings who genuinely and honestly believed, as we did, that what was signed in Helsinki was to be implemented and respected. Yet for those human beings incarcerated today in Poland, Czechoslovakia, the U.S.S.R. and other countries, Helsinki became a trap in which they were caught because they had faith and confidence that the world would lend them some legal protection when they, as members of public organizations, sought to do what the accords themselves demanded of them and promised they could do.
What irony, Mr. Speaker, that in the course of the deliberations of this parliament of free men, a parliamentarian such as I can only find seven minutes to decry the plight of human beings serving a total of approximately 150 years of incarceration, human beings who have risked their lives to entrench fundamental human rights and civil liberties for their peoples, the principles of brotherhood, of justice and of peace, in their countries, and who are now serving prison terms of up to 15 years! I refer to all the arrested members of the Helsinki Public Monitoring Groups in Russia, Ukraine, Lithuania, Armenia, Georgia, Poland, Czechoslovakia and other countries: To name only a few, they are: Victoras Petkus, Gajaus-kas Palys, Mykola Rudenko, Oleksa Tykhyj, Myroslav Marynovych, Mykola Matusevych, Levko Lukianenko, Petro Vins, Yuri Orlov, Anatoly Shcharansky, Alexander Ginsburg, Zviad Gomsakhurdia, Merad Kostava, among many others.
Among the proposals jointly submitted by our Canadian delegation and 14 other states in Belgrade, the participating states recognized the right of individuals and organizations to point out to their governments instances of non-implementation of the accords. If this was indeed our proposal, then it is our duty to ensure that, prior to the Madrid conference, such individuals as I have mentioned are granted legal protection to monitor the implementation of the Helsinki accords, in freedom, without persecution, and that those who have been arrested be released. If that is not done, the final act itself will
Adjournment Debate
be a mere circus, and all credibility in detente will be destroyed, not only among the participatory states but, above all, among the citizens of every country, among them the citizens of Canada.
Canada's position prior to and at the Madrid conference must change drastically so as to expose, protest, and condemn openly and without shame and hesitation, to stand firmly on our principles in our protest against those regimes for whom diplomacy, unfortunately, is but a game of lies and deceit in pursuit of their political and international interests.
I should like to point out that very often this demands a sacrifice on the part of Canadian citizens, the sacrifice perhaps of our economic expediency. When I see that the Canadian Export Development Corporation has extended to the Soviet Union over $500 million in credit, or that $9.3 million worth of Canadian oil equipment is being sold to the Soviet Union, I conclude that there might be some economic expediency in our silence. I must remind the House that President Carter placed an embargo on the sale of computers. He demanded that the sale of oil equipment should be granted a presidential veto when Shcharansky was arrested. He took a drastic and open stand with regard to the arrests of these individuals who were incarcerated and caged because they believe in Helsinki. We have a moral responsibility toward them. It will demand a sacrifice, and there is no question that serious decisions will have to be made, but if political and economic expediency becomes the base and foundation in our diplomatic relations with human beings and countries, we will be moving in the direction of the Orwellian world of 1984 where human beings became mere robots, mere machines dependent on the fickle will of the state. Such is the trend in many regimes.
I appeal to this parliament of free men to emphasize before the government and before our citizens that a drastic change must be made. There is no question that the Madrid conference will be held at the same time as the Moscow Olympics. The Soviet government is faced with the decision either to arrest these people en masse or to free them en masse. Our stand can save them, and can release the incarcerated.

speakeroldname: Mr. Louis Duclos (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-GOVERNMENT'S INSTRUCTIONS TO CANADIAN DELEGATION AT BELGRADE CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to throw some light on the instructions given to the Canadian delegation which will represent Canada at an international conference on the Helsinki Accords to be held in Madrid. I would, by the same token, reply to a question raised in the House yesterday by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Shymko).
The Canadian delegation to the Belgrade conference had received instructions reflecting the particular importance the Canadian government and the Canadian people attach to the provisions of the Final Act of the Helsinki Accords concerning human rights and other humane matters. We did not give specific instructions urging our delegation to avoid mentioning the names of victims and violators in cases such as those

March 1, 1979
Adjournment Debate
involving members of the Helsinki Accords monitoring groups in the Soviet Union. We did ask the delegation, however, to frame its interventions in objective and impartial terms and to endeavour to maintain a climate in which a dialogue would remain possible without controversy or confrontation.
Past experience has taught us that discreet representations usually give better results than forceful statements. Of course, we are tempted to make party politics with those matters, Mr. Speaker, but any person who is aware of his responsibilities and who has a minimum of experience in international matters and diplomacy knows full well that vociferous statements are not very fruitful as a rule. Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that the hon. member will agree that both the victims and those who made such violations could not ignore the position of Canada on those matters.
Besides, if the hon. member read the statements of the Canadian delegation, and in particular that of October 31, 1977, as reproduced in the brochure Canada At Belgrade which was published after the conference, he will realize-I am pleased to see that he has already read it-that Canada has never concealed its positions. With regard to individual cases implicating the Soviet Union, special instructions were given to our delegation: it was asked to underline to the Soviet delegation the concern of both our government and the Canadian people, and to present our proposals for solving those unfortunate cases.
